Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.27020v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We examine whether social trust shapes the pricing of lottery-like stocks by influencing investors' beliefs regarding optimistic information associated with extreme future payoffs. We argue that higher social trust reduces investors' skepticism toward optimistic information associated with extreme future payoffs, increasing demand for lottery-type stocks and leading to overpricing and lower subsequent returns. Using a sample of 8,875 firms across 49 US states over the period 1996-2018 and MAX as a proxy for lottery-like characteristics, we show that the MAX effect is concentrated in regions with relatively high trust and is weak or absent in regions with relatively low trust. We further find that this trust conditioning is stronger in regions with lower education or income levels, consistent with social trust playing a relatively more notable role when investors have more limited access to private information. The results are robust to alternative lottery proxies and a range of robustness checks. Our findings identify social trust as a novel determinant of the pricing of lottery-like stocks and provide evidence that social capital may amplify belief-driven mispricing in assets with highly skewed payoffs.

In a recent development, amazon Connect Customer enhances service level agreements (SLAs) for cases, so teams can set service goals for more of their work and respond faster when a case falls behind. Admins can set SLAs on case fields beyond status, such as requiring a case’s severity to drop from high to medium within 24 hours. Admins can add an email action to SLA breach rules, so the assigned agent learns right away when a case misses its SLA. Developers can use APIs to adjust a case’s SLA deadline when the team is waiting on information from an outside party, such as a partner.

Industry observers note that cases is available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (London), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Africa (Cape Town). To learn more and get started, visit the Cases webpage and documentation.

DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles.
  • The model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window.
  • According to recent reports, we recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles. We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%. Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks.

The checkpoints are available under Apache 2.0:.

The model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window. The longer training sessions use harness summarization to span multiple trajectories. See the model card for model properties and inference settings.

According to recent reports, we recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding. The SGLang cookbook provides launch configurations for different GPUs and checkpoint formats.

After starting the server with the served model name DaisyRose-27B on port 30000, you can send a request using the OpenAI Python client:.

It has been revealed that the model thinks before answering by default. Its reasoning is returned in reasoning_content, and its final answer in content. These settings follow the model card’s quickstart.

In a recent development, daisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, where pass@1 rises from 5.6% to 12.0%.

Sources indicate that scores use the higher of the BF16 and FP8 runs for each benchmark; the two differ by less than one point wherever both were evaluated. The model card includes comparison sources and evaluation settings.

Three parts of the training setup made this release possible: carefully designed tasks, an efficient training backend, and reliable sandboxes.

We built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI, starting from its large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 made it into the final training set.

We selected tasks using three criteria:.

RadixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. The learning runs on our internal training backend, which is built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens, folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization.

57% lower training cost. On this release, 37% of each GPU’s peak compute went into useful training work (model FLOPs utilization, or MFU) on our backend. The open-source trainer, built on Megatron, reached 16% on comparable runs. So the same training needs 57% less GPU time. The gain is even larger on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash.

2× faster end to end. Counting the time the agent spends on its tasks, the release run trained on about 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs. The open-source trainer reached about 8,300 on the same GPUs.

Stable over weeks. The release run trained for weeks on 144 H200s, 63,000 GPU-hours in total. From the first step to the last, its speed and efficiency held steady.

In a recent development, every training step of the DaisyRose-27B release run on 144 H200s, plotted against total training time. Dashed lines: the open-source trainer on comparable runs.

Every training attempt runs in a sandbox: a fresh copy of the task’s environment where the agent runs commands, edits files, and is then graded.

Our service is built on the open-source AgentENV project, to which we also contribute fixes. Between mid-September and mid-November, it ran about 944,000 sandboxes for this project, with up to 1,566 running concurrently.

Industry observers note that the service grew from one machine to as many as 12. We shipped ten upgrades to it, nearly all while training was running. Across all nine weeks, 99% of sandbox creations succeeded; since late October, that figure has exceeded 99.95%.

Industry observers note that cloud infrastructure costs for the project’s sandboxes were about 80% lower than running the same sandboxes with popular cloud sandbox providers. One way we keep costs down is to let each sandbox’s memory allocation grow and shrink with its actual usage, allowing more sandboxes to share each machine.

Download DaisyRose-27B, follow the SGLang serving guide, or use Miles to train your own agents.

We’d like to hear how DaisyRose-27B performs on your tasks, including where it falls short. Share your setup and results in the model’s Community tab.

Industry observers note that we thank Eigent AI for working closely with us on training data, and the Qwen team for creating Qwen3.8-27B. We also thank the Miles and SGLang communities, along with other open-source projects including slime, AgentENV, and Harbor.

Are Calibrated Decision Models Calibrated on Markets? Geolocated News, Markov Switching and a System One Model for Nasdaq-100 Allocation

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (324 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.26716v1 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: Portfolio allocation is driven by probabilities of losses, not only by forecasts of the direction (up/down) of the market. A decision model such as Jev returns a probability for a yes/no question and has been reported to be well calibrated on a set of benchmarks. However, the model's calibration against realised market outcomes has not been tested. In this study, every Friday we ask whether the Nasdaq-100 will close lower four weeks later and compare a two-regime Markov-switching model estimated on data from 1990 to 2026, Jev reading weekly headlines and geolocated news features computed with spatial queries in PostGIS, and their combination. A knowledge probe reveals that Jev knows events up to late 2024, so we evaluate it on 88 weeks from January 2025 onwards. None of the models predicts the direction better than the historical base rate. A key finding is that raw Jev overestimates the probability of a decline: its mean forecast is 0.48 against an observed frequency of 0.38, and its ECE is 0.10. A prior shift to the historical base rate, which uses no outcomes from the test period, lowers the ECE to 0.015. In contrast, Platt scaling, isotonic regression and the combination with the Markov model all make the forecasts worse. In a half-Kelly allocation, the raw Jev strategy returns 3.1% per year, whereas after the prior shift it returns 14.5%; a simple buy-and-hold strategy in QQQ returns 15.3% per year. The Markov model forecasts large declines (more than 10%) well, with an AUC of 0.81, and its strategy has the highest Sharpe ratio over 1999-2026. Asked about such a large decline (base rate 4%), raw Jev forecasts 16-24% on average, and the same prior shift removes this offset. The practical lesson is that decision-model probabilities must be anchored to the base rate of the market event before they are used to size positions.

#23993. Tech Report: The most misunderstood graph in AI just got a major update

Tech Report: The most misunderstood graph in AI just got a major update

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1318 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding.
  • The report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared—and widely misinterpreted, owing to the complexity of the measures it used.
  • It has been revealed that the updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than those in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding.

The report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared—and widely misinterpreted, owing to the complexity of the measures it used. METR evaluated models by having them attempt a large suite of tasks, each of which had also been completed by humans. Each task’s difficulty was scored by how long it took the human testers to finish it—and then models were rated according to the length of the tasks that they could complete. That plot showed that AI systems were rapidly improving—every four months, the length of the tasks that frontier models could successfully complete doubled.

It has been revealed that the updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than those in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended. One of the biggest questions in AI right now is the extent to which progress on “verifiable” tasks—where it’s possible to check automatically whether an AI system has succeeded or failed—carry over into tasks on which success or failure is harder to measure. We know how to teach neural networks how to do verifiable tasks: Researchers have the systems attempt one many times, strengthen the neural pathways that contribute to success, and weaken the pathways that contribute to failures. That’s why AI systems have become so good at coding and math, two domains where it’s possible to determine automatically whether a solution does or doesn’t work.

It’s much harder to apply this technique, known as reinforcement learning, to tasks where success is less well defined or takes longer to ascertain—such as choosing a latest research direction. For the same reason, it’s tough to evaluate AI performance on these tasks, so METR’s original time horizon plot didn’t include any of them. But it’s precisely this type of task that will prove essential if AI systems are to automate research and development.

Recent findings suggest that and AI research and development is an especially hot topic right now. Parts of the AI community are still reeling from a different, heavily redacted METR report from earlier this month, which claimed that AI might be speeding up the pace of AI progress at Anthropic by a factor of two. That report sparked fears that the company (which just had a blockbuster IPO) could soon achieve full recursive self-improvement, a regime in which AI systems autonomously design their own successors with no human involvement.

It has been revealed that METR researchers have worked to make sure their new suite of tasks includes some of the fuzzier, judgment-laden ones that could be most relevant to AI research and development. In one task, they ask models to design new AI evaluations that METR could use in its research and then have human METR employees score the results. Even though the most advanced models are now better than almost every human at software engineering, here they fall short: Not one of the AI-designed evaluations was good enough for METR employees to consider it useful for their research.

Industry observers note that in another task, models have to score philosophical arguments. This task is intended to capture the extent to which models can exercise good judgment—though METR writes in the report that employees disagree about how relevant the task is for automation of AI R&D. On this task, too, models fell short of human performance.

According to recent reports, though it’s difficult to score these latest tasks—and even harder to determine what the scores mean—experts I spoke with appreciate that METR is incorporating new types of evaluations into its work. “We’re at the point where AI evaluations need to get more creative,” notes Sayash Kapoor, a computer scientist and incoming professor at UC Berkeley. “Trying to push the envelope of the space of evaluations is a welcome change.”.

In a recent development, kapoor claims he wasn’t surprised to see that models fall short of performance on more open-ended tasks, such as designing an AI evaluation—in a preprint from August, he and his collaborators reported that AI models are not yet able to reproduce human computer science research on their own. And in a Wednesday blog post, OpenAI reported that its models don’t do as well on the real-world tasks its employees assign them as they do on the easier, more verifiable tasks in METR’s original suite.

In a recent development, still, people disagree about how to interpret current performance differences on easily verifiable and hard-to-verify tasks, Kapoor says. Though he thinks that research taste—the ability to choose promising questions, hypotheses, and experiments—will prove a major bottleneck in automating AI R&D, others contend that models trained on easy-to-verify tasks will eventually be able to successfully complete open-ended tasks as well. And progress on verifiable tasks doesn’t seem to be slowing down.

Even if the models do lag behind human performance on open-ended tasks right now, the newly introduced report suggests that they might be getting better. Some of the newest models, such as Opus 5.5, tend to achieve what METR calls “borderline above the bar” performance on the evaluation design tasks—not yet usable for METR's research, but promising. Just a year ago, every model was scoring in the “clearly below the bar” category.

According to recent reports, but because these open-ended and judgment-heavy tasks are so tough to design and score, METR includes few of them in its report, and that makes it difficult to predict whether and how models might continue to progress in these areas. “The improvement we observe, I think that does tell us something for the current moment,” says Najoung Kim, a linguist and computer scientist at Boston University. “I’m not sure just yet how to think about how it would extrapolate.”.

In a recent development, matt Putz, a member of the technical staff at METR, notes that predicting progress on these kinds of tasks is likely to remain difficult. “By their nature, hard-to-verify or judgment-laden tasks are much harder to study, and especially to quantify,” he noted in an email. “Ultimately, I don’t think we’ll be able to establish trends as clean and robust as for the easy-to-specify [tasks].”.

According to recent reports, in general, METR is clearly butting up against the practical difficulties of testing AI performance on difficult and underspecified tasks—precisely the ones most relevant to automating AI R&D. METR’s time horizon plots score task difficulty by evaluating how long it would take a human to complete the task, and for the original plot they measured this quantity by actually having people try each task.

In a recent development, in the new report, however, the completion times are mostly estimates, because paying people for tasks that might take hundreds of hours, or that only a few experts are qualified to complete, is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming. Other tasks have more specific shortcomings—for example, for the philosophical argument task, just one person rated most of the arguments, and agents are judged by how well they agree with that particular individual. It’s possible that the scores would change if more experts were surveyed—but that, too, is time-consuming.

According to recent reports, it’s still early days for evaluating models on tasks that are hard to validate or require judgment. And while the experts I spoke with see the inclusion of these tasks in METR’s newest time horizon plot as a clear step in the right direction, they agree that we are still far from achieving any definitive answers about whether, and how quickly, automated AI R&D might be coming. “This move toward open-ended tasks is promising,” Kapoor says. But, he adds, “there is just such a lot more to be done to actually get a fuller understanding.”.

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.26700v1 Announce Type: latest Abstract: This paper studies how accounting-induced opacity affects systemic risk in the banking system. Motivated by the buildup of unrealized losses during recent monetary tightening episodes, we develop a model in which banks hold correlated interest rate sensitive assets and are connected through an endogenous interbank network. We show that Held-To-Maturity (HTM) accounting amplifies systemic risk by delaying loss recognition, allowing losses to accumulate and become synchronized across institutions. When losses are realized under liquidity stress, the interaction of correlated exposures and network linkages generates nonlinear increases in defaults. These findings suggest that accounting regimes are not neutral from a financial stability perspective, as they influence both the buildup and propagation of systemic risk, particularly in environments with common asset exposures and strong interconnectedness.

Latest Update: Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3833 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution.
  • It has been revealed that models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing.
  • Recent findings suggest that take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution.

It has been revealed that models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing. Instead, they target general performance. So when you combine a model and harness, you’re leaving performance and efficiency on the table for the stuff you’re actually doing. With RL, you can train a custom harness adapter that squeezes everything out of your model for your harness and task combination.

Recent findings suggest that take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task. If we freeze those weights and add a custom RL-trained LoRA adapter we can get 55% pass@1, with average token usage of 1.5K. Most of this is down to the model reasoning less, calling less tools, and performing better first time.

Sources indicate that our earlier work (multi-harness RL, harness adapters) demonstrated that RL on your own task distribution, inside your own harness, gives a more accurate and more efficient model. Those experiments covered data-analysis and code-building tasks. Here we wanted to push this further by exploring whether the result holds at 27B, on harder real-world software engineering tasks, across three harnesses: Pi, OpenCode and Hermes Agent. And most of all, share a fully reusable recipe, so you can reproduce this on your own task, harness, model combinations.

We leverage the Harbor integration in OpenEnv and TRL’s OpenEnv guide to train the model inside the harnesses we chose for the final training. We have built ready-to-use docker images for all our RL tasks that come with the target harnesses already pre-installed inside. In our final docker images, we use Pi 1.5.2, OpenCode 2.2.7 and Hermes Agent v0.22.6. The diagram below from the aforementioned blogpost explains well the entire protocol:.

Sources indicate that most RL frameworks train a re-implementation of the agent loop: the agent is written against the framework's own interface, such as verl's AgentLoop, SkyRL-Gym environments, rLLM's agent and environment classes, slime's custom rollout functions, or ART's client inside your own Python agent. Here the harness runs exactly as it ships, and the trainer learns from the exact tokens it produced, recorded by a proxy between the harness and vLLM. Recent work moves in the same direction: Agent Lightning v1.0 keeps the deploy-time harness in the loop through a proxy ("harnessed agentic RL"), and SkyRL's Harbor integration trains on Harbor trials, converting their chat histories into tokens for the trainer.

For this recipe we created a custom dataset for agentic coding with the Hub, OpenEnv, and Repo2RLEnv. We combined together task retrieval of existing RL envs, task generation with Repo2RLEnv, task validation with OpenEnv, and sampling into a single data pipeline. This gave us the highest quality set of validated and relevant tasks to improve Qwen3.8-27B on agentic coding. In this section, we’ll walk through how we built it, so you can try it out on your own domains.

RL training needs tasks the agent can attempt, a verifier that scores each attempt, and evidence that the verifier is right. A verifier that accepts wrong answers teaches the wrong behavior. A task that is already feasible will not teach the model anything.

This section describes how we built the task set from three sources: two on the Hugging Face Hub and a third generated with Tasksmith, a pipeline in Repo2RLEnv. Every task passes an eligibility screen with openenv validate, and the same difficulty check against the base model, Qwen3.8-27B.

According to recent reports, each task uses the Harbor format, which Terminal-Bench 2.1 also uses. A broad search of the Hub for Harbor environments returned about 59,000 tasks, but they included duplicates, evaluation sets and tasks marked as not for training. We filtered down to just two Hub sources built for training and generated a third set ourselves:.

According to recent reports, we used Tasksmith to target gaps. We mapped the skills that our target benchmarks test (Terminal-Bench 2.1, the hard subset of SWE-bench Pro, and DeepSWE), then chose pull requests that exercise them, such as HTTP streaming, filesystem operations and serialization. From 30 merged pull requests, Tasksmith produced 24 tasks in 10 Python repositories that passed its checks, 17 of them on a second run. Its checks do not replace ours, so these tasks go through the same pipeline as the rest.

A metadata screen runs first. It keeps tasks from training splits with permissive licenses. It drops duplicates, tasks marked as not for training, the 253 tasks in our target benchmarks, and any task from a repository those benchmarks use. We then ran the semantic checks from openenv validate on every task in fresh trials:.

Industry observers note that each trial ran as its own Hugging Face Job, which let us validate dozens of tasks at once. openenv validate offers the same option for any Harbor task:.

858 of 1,127 Hub candidates passed. Wrong-answer controls caught defects, including a Tasksmith task that accepted an incomplete implementation and a Terminal-Bench 2.1 verifier (regex-log) that accepted known-wrong answers. Most failures were infrastructure problems, such as images that did not start. Failed tasks stay in a rejected split with the failing check recorded.

A valid task can still teach nothing. GRPO (group relative policy optimization) scores each attempt against the other attempts at the same task, so a task where every attempt passes, or every attempt fails, gives no learning signal. Before training, Qwen3.8-27B attempted each task 4 times, or 8 times for a stratified sample of six tasks per repository.

Sources indicate that of 442 scored tasks, Qwen3.8-27B solved 151 every time and 120 never. The 171 tasks it solved only sometimes form the qualified set. The figure below shows how the scores pile up at both ends and how they differ by source. The model solves most Go tasks every time, fails every attempt on more than a third of the SWE-smith Python tasks, and lands in the middle on 73% of the SWE-Gym tasks.

Qwen3.8-27B results on 442 scored tasks. Green marks the qualified tasks, which the model solves on some attempts but not all.

This example demonstrates how we filtered and validated 1,127 tasks to 278 which we included directly in the final dataset. The pipeline then took the remaining 522 rejected tasks, repaired and complexified them with Tasksmith and repeated validation.

The pipeline applies two filters: validation removes broken tasks, and the difficulty check keeps tasks the base model solves only sometimes. This section tests whether those filters change what the model learns. We trained four short runs of up to 50 steps, each on tasks from a different stage of the pipeline, and compared them with the base model on Terminal-Bench 2.1.

Industry observers note that each run trains Qwen3.8-27B with LoRA and GRPO, using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer, on 32 tasks. All four use the same agent harness (OpenCode with up to 48 model calls), the same settings and one 8×H200 Hugging Face Job, and the reward is the verifier's pass or fail. The task sets differ in how they were filtered:.

According to recent reports, the figure below shows how the tasks impacted model learning. The table lists each run's steps and the checkpoint we evaluate. The chart tracks training reward across subsets of tasks with differing validation status.

Industry observers note that harness-hub/agentic-coding-envs holds 871 tasks from 35 repositories. Hub tasks are capped at 40 per repository, so no single project dominates. The table below shows what each source contributes. The dataset has two views: every accepted task, and the qualified subset for GRPO training. Rejected attempts stay in a separate config.

We leveraged the stable version of AsyncGRPOTrainer from TRL, with the main advantage of the trainer being that it does not wait until all rollouts are completed before moving to the next training optimization step.

For more detailed reading on the trainer and its building blocks, please refer to the AsyncGRPO blogpost.

To obtain our final harness adapters, we trained LoRA adapters on top of Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer. The adapters were attached to the model using the all-linear flag. To maximize the training efficiency, thinking mode was turned off during rollout stages, and we evaluated our final adapter with and without thinking for broader comparison.

The final reward function consists of the verifier's correctness, combined with a small tool-efficiency bonus (0.1, derived from early experiments from the previous iteration of harness adapters which highlighted that 0.1 worked best).

We performed a small LR sweep on 50 steps using Termgrade environments (1e-5, 5e-5 and 1e-4) and noticed that 1e-5 barely moved training correctness (from 0.52 to 0.50), 1e-4 collapsed the rollouts instead of improving them (turns per rollout moved from 18 to 6, with entropy rising), and only 5e-5 clearly improved (from 0.49 to 0.60 by step 40). Longer 5e-5 runs then indicated signs of instability (collapsing rollout lengths, rising entropy), so we settled on 2e-5 for the final runs.

According to recent reports, each harness adapter was trained using NVIDIA 2xB200 GPUs, with one GPU allocated for the vLLM server and the other allocated for the training process. We first performed some stress testing to maximize the amount of RL tasks that can be trained within a single optimization step. For that, we ‘maxed out’ the --token-budget argument from AsyncGRPOTrainer to its limit for the setup that we had. The chart below demonstrates the evolution of the number of groups per step for each harness (in blue: Pi, green: OpenCode and orange: Hermes).

As the model gets better and better during training, it is able to fit more and more groups during each training step, which diversifies the signals that the model gets at each optimization step.

Sources indicate that the final data mixture consists of 750 tasks from harness-adapters RL environments and 300 tasks from termgrade. In order to maximize the diversity of the sampled tasks during training, we have slightly customized the data sampling strategy, which will be explained below:.

Before training, the tasks are put in a fixed order that interleaves them by family (i.e., their repository for our generated RL environments. For Termgrade, we just sorted them by name since each task is considered as its own family), so every training step mixes as many repositories as possible while following the distribution of the mixture.

Industry observers note that we also plug the safeagents tool, in order to block any misbehavior from the model during training. The final plugin (which consists of the regex and pattern rules specific to the RL tasks and test path) is hosted in harness-hub/qwen-safeagents-plugin and can be used out of the box using the latest version of safeagents in case anyone wants to reproduce the training setup.

The number of blocked tools from safeagents decreases consistently during training, which indicates that the model gets ‘safer and safer’ after each optimization step. Below is a diagram of the safeagents blocked calls per 1000 tool calls, by training step, for each harness adapter.

According to recent reports, merging models often combines their capabilities while keeping most of what each one could do. Once the three harness adapters were trained, we asked two questions. Does merging them cost accuracy? And can a single "super-adapter" be accurate and efficient under every harness?

We started by comparing the weight updates of the three adapters, layer by layer. The cosine similarity between any two of them is about 0.01–0.02: each adapter pushed the model in a nearly orthogonal direction during training. That's the best case for merging, since the updates barely interfere.

According to recent reports, we concatenate the three LoRA adapters along the rank dimension (PEFT's combination_type="cat"). The merged adapter has rank 96 (3 × 32) and applies exactly w · (ΔW_pi + ΔW_hermes + ΔW_opencode). Prior work on merging (task arithmetic, TIES, KnOTS) finds that scaling each update below 1 works best, so we compared three weights on all 89 Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks, under each harness, with the step-120 adapters:.

Industry observers note that the plain sum over-applies the updates. The agents become very short (13 tool calls per task, against 49 for the base model), and while Hermes peaks at 62.8%, pi falls back to the base model's level. The average dilutes each harness's own patch. ½ gives the best balance, so we built the final super-adapter from the released checkpoints (pi step 160, hermes step 160, opencode step 150) at weight ½.

Under each harness, on the tasks every run graded (50–51 on SWE-bench Pro, 82–85 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), one attempt per task (in parentheses, the efficiency gain with respect to the base model):.

"Thinking" is the chat template's thinking mode at its default effort (xhigh). The specialists were trained and served with thinking off.

With thinking off, the super-adapter improves on the base model on all six harness–benchmark pairs (mean pass@1 39.5% → 49.0%; 71 tasks newly solved vs 34 lost, p < 0.001).

Despite not being trained at all with thinking on, it's the strongest model we evaluated with thinking mode. Against the base model thinking at the same effort, it wins on five of six pairs and ties the sixth (mean 55.5% → 63.5%; 67 newly solved vs 37 lost, p = 0.004). The largest gains are on SWE-bench Pro: +16 points under hermes and +20 under opencode. Under pi on SWE-bench Pro, where thinking alone already reaches 74%, it ties.

Use the specialist harness adapters when thinking off. Each harness's own adapter is ahead on four of six pairs, by the most under pi (64.0% vs 46.0% on SWE-bench Pro, 56.5% vs 48.2% on Terminal-Bench). Splitting one model across three harnesses costs pi the most of its gain. If you only use one harness and keep thinking off, take its specialist.

According to recent reports, the super adapter is also much more efficient. On the tasks both the base model and the super-adapter solve, with thinking off, it makes 53–73% fewer tool calls and generates 44–60% fewer tokens per task, with fewer tool calls on 111 of 130 tasks. With thinking on, it still cuts tool calls by 31–48% and tokens by 24–43% on SWE-bench Pro. On Terminal-Bench, tool calls drop by 19–25% and token counts stay about the same.

According to recent reports, the ½ weight was chosen on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the step-120 adapters, so the Terminal-Bench numbers are slightly optimistic; SWE-bench Pro played no part in the choice. Full paired results are in the super-adapter's model card.

This section reports what happened during training, then how the adapters score on held-out benchmarks inside and outside their own harnesses.

Training ran for a cumulative total of 598 steps, with a total of 78,114 samples trained, which consists exactly of 167M trained tokens.

During training, we see a clear signal that the model learns to solve tasks in fewer and fewer steps, with no clear sign of saturation. Despite having some clear increasing trend sometimes, training correctness seems to overall stay flat. This can be explained by the fact that the model meets new tasks during training, but the number of groups that fit in a step’s token budget more than doubles as trajectories get shorter. The accuracy gains show up on the held-out benchmarks in the section below.

In a recent development, on the other hand, safeagents was able to block multiple suspicious attempts. Across the three training runs, a total of 1.3M tool calls have been checked, and a total of 647 tool calls have been blocked.

This section covers the evaluation setup, the in-harness results, transfer across harnesses, and an out-of-distribution check.

We evaluate each adapter inside the harness it was trained in, on two agentic coding benchmarks: all 89 tasks of Terminal-Bench 2.1 (1 hour and 100 agent steps per task) and the 51 hardest tasks of SWE-bench Pro (2 hours and 100 agent steps). We cap the maximum number of tokens per task to be 131072. We do not tune the agent settings and use the default setup for all harnesses. For example, Pi automatically applies context compaction, while OpenCode and Hermes don't, which mainly affects the SWE-bench Pro results due to rapid context overflow. Therefore you cannot compare the results across different harnesses (using Pi does not necessarily lead to better results than Hermes or OpenCode), but it is fair to compare results within the same harness and draw conclusions.

Recent findings suggest that every rollout runs through the same Harbor and OpenEnv stack as training, in HF sandboxes, with one attempt per task at temperature 0.8 and thinking off. Each LoRA checkpoint is merged into the base weights and served alone with vLLM on a single GPU, at the same concurrency as the base model's eval.

For all the evaluation benchmarks, we report the pass@1 as well as the number of tool calls, total turns, for all tasks and for solved tasks.

For openness, all model trajectories for final evaluations are pushed in this public bucket: harness-hub/harness-adapters-trajectories.

According to recent reports, all three specialist adapters beat the base model under their own harness, on both benchmarks. On SWE-bench Pro (hard 51), pi goes from 39.2% to 64.7% (+25.5 points: 15 tasks newly solved vs 2 lost, p = 0.002), hermes from 29.4% to 43.1%, and opencode from 35.3% to 51.0%. On the full Terminal-Bench 2.1, pi gains +16.3 points (16 vs 2, p = 0.001) and hermes +14.1 (19 vs 7, p = 0.03). Opencode gains +6.0 overall, and +13.6 on the 66 tasks that played no part in choosing its checkpoint (12 vs 3, p = 0.035).

It has been revealed that the adapters also solve tasks much more efficiently: on the tasks both they and the base model solve, they make 56–72% fewer tool calls per task on SWE-bench Pro and 53–70% fewer on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The single super-adapter beats the base model under all three harnesses too (+6 to +18 points on SWE-bench Pro, +5 to +10 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), with just as large a cut in tool calls (53–73%). It keeps less of each specialist's gain with thinking off, most under pi, but with thinking on it beats the base model thinking at the same effort on five of six harness–benchmark pairs (see the super-adapter section). Each model card has the full paired results.

To answer this question, we also evaluated the pi harness adapter under Hermes Agent and OpenCode.

Under OpenCode it matches OpenCode's own specialist on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (44.8% → 54.0%, against 46.4% → 52.4%). Under Hermes it keeps about two-thirds of the specialist's gain (46.3% → 56.1%, against 44.7% → 58.8%), with the same ~45% cut in tool calls in both. Therefore it seems that the newly learned capabilities are transferred across harnesses.

What happens if we evaluate in out-of-distribution tasks, outside the harnesses the adapters have been trained with?

We ran all five models on 300 AutomationBench tasks which consists of business-automation workflows evaluations, with AutomationBench's own agent loop instead of Pi, Hermes or OpenCode. This way, we can cross check two different questions: can the model solve problems outside SWE-related tasks? What happens when the model is being put outside the harness it has been trained with?

Results show that the adapters stay close to the base model. Pi and OpenCode are slightly ahead (27.0% and 25.3% pass@1 against 23.0%), the merged adapter is level (23.7%), and Hermes is a few points behind (17.7%). The differences are within noise, except perhaps Hermes, therefore RL inside the harnesses neither transfers clearly to this very different setting nor breaks the model on it.

It has been revealed that we appreciate the feedback from the users and the community, initial testing and results from the community seemed overall extremely positive, and we wish to continue in this direction in the future. We also saw some surprising results, such as users reporting that the harness adapters work really well under Qwen3.8 derivatives, such as Swift-1.5.

According to recent reports, this question is an open question we thought about, post-release. After inspecting carefully the generated trajectories from the evaluation benchmarks, it turns out the model, under non-thinking mode, tends to generate some short text before proposing a tool call, as opposed to the base model which generates the tool calls barely without any text beforehand.

Sources indicate that this phenomenon can be seen as a sort of ‘reasoning leakage’, where the model learns to ‘escape’ from its non-thinking version to its thinking version by generating some text that can sometimes look like reasoning traces (e.g.: ..wait? ..let me see, etc.). A recent paper also describes behavior from LLMs during the RL stage very well.

Does this invalidate our models? We do not think so, as the final results are still valid; under the exact same conditions (fixed token budget) our adapters do outperform the base non-thinking model (by far) and match the performance of the thinking version, while being much more token efficient. This has been further confirmed by the positive feedback from the community.

Industry observers note that however this raises the need of a proper follow up work, where we will try to re-apply the same pipeline for pure thinking models, as well as exploring hybrid thinking / non-thinking training, to better understand the behavior of RL training on hybrid thinking models. We will share with the community our next findings (and harness adapters), once we get conclusive results.

Throughout this work, we demonstrated that RL training your model inside your target harness leads to more efficient and therefore more accurate final models, when evaluated under the same conditions. This observation is in line and in continuation with several previous work from Hugging Face teams, such as multi-harness-RL or the early iterations of harness adapters.

In the future, we will explore applying this recipe to more models, while better studying the training strategies for hybrid thinking / non-thinking models.

Recent findings suggest that we also share to the community openly the full recipe and pipeline to reproduce everything, and invite everyone to build their own RL tasks, derived from their own codebase, or any relevant materials, and apply the same training recipe and ideas to their favorite model and harness for more efficient agentic models. We hope this blogpost will serve as a starting point for builders to build and share their own harness adapters in the future.

Industry observers note that thanks for such a nice and detailed blog on it. Can you also share, how many iterations did this take, and roughly how long end to end? What would be the minimum GPU requirements to train. Also curious how you think the adapter holds up when the harness changes.

Nice article guys!For adapters merging, one cool idea would be to do MOPD where the student is Qwen3.8-27B (the original one) and teachers are the RL lora adapted one. The random selection of the harness selects the teacher.

Latest Update: Error analysis for the numerical approximation of the quantile hedging problem

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (203 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.26673v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: We analyse numerical approximations of quantile hedging in complete linear markets with Markovian diffusion dynamics. The problem is formulated as stochastic control for an augmented state $(X,P)$, where the probability martingale $P$ is constrained to $[0,1]$ and controlled through an unbounded volatility coefficient. We combine control truncation with piecewise-constant policy time-stepping (PCPT), stopping controls continuously upon boundary hitting to preserve the state constraint. Using one-step dynamic programming principles and regularisation, we derive a generator inequality and explicit value-function error bounds. Under standard coefficient regularity and a Lipschitz payoff, optimising the truncation and regularisation parameters yields an error exponent arbitrarily close to $1/8$ from below, uniformly in the probability variable. For controls bounded from the outset, we obtain exponents arbitrarily close to $1/4$ from below, approaching the exponent established by Jakobsen, Picarelli and Reisinger without state constraints. We also implement a fully discrete scheme with neural-network controls. Grid-time projection onto $[0,1]$ introduces a martingale defect and a pricing bias. We quantify this bias in a toy problem and mitigate it using a state-dependent control bound. Experiments in Black--Scholes and Lipschitz local-volatility models illustrate the correction and the decrease in pricing errors under grid refinement.

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.26670v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: This paper develops a Solvency II-based pricing framework for structural longevity risk in incomplete longevity markets. The valuation scheme relies on the Cost-of-Capital principle underlying the Risk Margin and combines it with a continuous-time affine mortality model. Mortality dynamics are specified in calendar time, with age-dependent mortality patterns linked to a latent longevity factor driving long-term mortality improvements. The affine structure preserves closed-form survival probabilities and provides a tractable basis for repeated Best Estimate, Solvency Capital Requirement and Risk Margin calculations. We derive the conditional distribution of one-year discounted Best Estimate variations, obtaining analytical expressions for their asymmetry and Value-at-Risk under the Gaussian affine specification. Within this setting, we introduce a stress-based assessment by applying adverse shocks to the deterministic parameters governing the longevity trend. The trend-based stress is compared with a mortality-level stress and with a Value-at-Risk-based capital assessment. The methodology links stochastic mortality modelling, prudential capital valuation and longevity-linked payoff assessment within a unified actuarial framework. A numerical application based on Belgian mortality data illustrates the implementation and shows that the mortality-level stress produces substantially larger scenario-based capital-cost measures than the trend-based stress. These findings highlight the sensitivity of longevity risk valuation to the specification of adverse mortality scenarios. The approach offers a transparent and operational basis for assessing and pricing structural longevity risk under a Solvency II Cost-of-Capital perspective.

  • TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a latest looped transformer model.
  • Sources indicate that inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups.
  • Sources indicate that we ship transformers, Llama App (llama.cpp), and MLX support.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a latest looped transformer model. It’s a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts with ~26B physical total and 3B active parameters per token. It uses a neat trick to increase capacity: some layers are visited in a loop that repeats three times, which makes it work like it had more parameters. It supports a 1M-token context size, accepts images and text inputs. Thinking Machines Lab ships the model in a mixed-precision format, with NVFP4 and MXFP8 expert weights. A DSpark drafter is also included for additional speed-up at a small memory cost.

Sources indicate that inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups. We think this is a refreshingly latest great local model. In our vibe tests, it's at least comparable with Qwen 3.8 27B. More validation is needed, but we are super excited about this release!

Sources indicate that we ship transformers, Llama App (llama.cpp), and MLX support. SGLang also provides day-zero inference support for production deployments on datacenter hardware.

This post goes through what makes Inkling Mini different, some of our vibe tests, and how you can use it with your setup.

According to recent reports, inkling 2 Mini is a mixture-of-experts model with 24 decoder layers, but the 12 middle layers run three times in a loop. Therefore, the model acts as if it had 48 (6+ 3*12 + 6) logical layers with just 24 physical ones.

According to recent reports, similar to Inkling 2 Small, Inkling 2 Mini executes 48 layer visits per token. The hidden size is 2,304 instead of 4,608. At each layer visit, both variants route the token to 8 experts, but Mini selects them from among 128 experts per layer, while Small selects from 384.The decoder runs layers 0–5 once, layers 6–17 three times, and layers 18–23 once. All three passes through layers 6–17 reuse the same weights.

Architectures such as Nanbeige have explored looping before. But Inkling 2 Mini explores an interesting approach. Every pass through the looped core (layers 6–17) starts from the same inputs which is the output of the first six layers. Information moves between passes through cross-pass messages. Each looped layer reads a message from the previous pass's outputs with its own learned query (one message for its query, key, value and MLP inputs). A small gating controller then looks at both the layer's current input and the message. It decides how much of the current input to forget and how much of the message to add. Each pass therefore refines what the previous one computed.

Text decoder width is 2,304, and the intermediate width of each expert is 1,152. Reusing core weights reduces the number of distinct layers the checkpoint stores. The model still executes all 48 visits, and each visit keeps its own KV and short-convolution state.

In addition to the flagship Inkling 2 Mini model, a research artifact has also been released. It shares the same architecture, but this variant was trained to accept a variable number of passes through the loop 🤯. Setting 1 or 2 passes instead of 3 will make inference run a lot faster, but generations may be of slightly lower quality. We tested this variant, and it works, but we haven’t evaluated it in depth.

Inkling 2 Mini is state-of-the-art in its class in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 (AAv5), as well as across many benchmarks in various categories. Compared with Gemma 4 31B, Muse Glimmer, Qwen3.8-27B, and Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, Inkling 2 Mini leads in 32 benchmarks out of 48. These cover coding and autoresearch, agentic search and tool use for knowledge work, vision interpretation and creation, reasoning and knowledge, and safety and alignment. See the Inkling 2 Mini model card for the full list of benchmarks and scores.

Inkling 2 Mini is a great local coding companion. It leads in FrontierCode v2.0, ties with Qwen3.8-27B on Terminal-Bench 4.0, and trails Qwen on AutomationBench-AA v1.0.6. You can check out a few of our highlights below for coding and knowledge work. Note that AA Briefcase is in ELO rating, higher is better.

According to recent reports, pass reasoning_effort="medium" to processor.apply_chat_template(...) to set the effort for a request. The chat template adds the numeric value to the prompt as a system message. The default is high (0.9).

Available levels are none (0.0), minimal (0.1), low (0.2), medium (0.7), high (0.9; default), xhigh (0.99), and max (0.99). You can also pass a number from 0.0 to 0.99, such as reasoning_effort=0.35.

Recent findings suggest that SGLang can use a three-layer DSpark draft to propose tokens for the target model to verify. The draft reads the inputs to decoder visits 5, 23, and 41, plus the final normalized state at index 48. With the draft weights present, add --speculative-algorithm DSPARK --context-length 131072 to the server command.

We benchmarked the models with and without speculative decoding, and measured generation speed on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU where every request has a 1,024-token prompt and generates exactly 1,024 tokens and concurrency of 1, 4, 16 and 64.

We upstreamed MLX support to the mlx-lm project, including multimodal image and text inputs, and shared quants through the mlx-community organization.

MLX inference works with the original checkpoint too. In this case, the native nvfp4 + mxfp8 quantization scheme is used without reconversion: you get the original quality the authors intended.

According to recent reports, build the most impressive original real-time scene you can: a slow, cinematic camera flight over procedural mountains, through volumetric clouds and low over water with reflections, all lit by a sunset. Deliver it as a single self-contained index.html in the current directory that renders everything in one full-screen WebGL fragment shader, purely from code (no textures, images, fonts, libraries, external files or network requests of any kind). It must run smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080, aiming for 60 fps on a desktop GPU, with an automatic resolution-scale fallback that lowers the internal render resolution when the frame rate drops, and the flight must keep going indefinitely without glitches. To check your work, run node shot.cjs index.html shot.png 6 (the third argument is how many seconds to wait; a comma list such as 3,12,25 saves one screenshot per time, and an optional fourth argument sets the size, default 1280x720): it renders the page in headless Chrome, saves the screenshot(s), and prints the WebGL renderer, a rough frame rate and any console errors; then look at the images. The headless renderer on this machine may be software-only, so its frame rate can be far below what a real desktop GPU achieves and is not the target. Decide for yourself when the result is finished, then reply with a short description of what you built.

Vincent van Gogh, The Starry Night (1889).

We gave Inkling 2 Mini a reference image of Van Gogh’s painting and a screenshot helper in the Pi coding harness. Inkling wrote a self-contained HTML page with a single WebGL2 fragment shader. Distributional Deep Hedging

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (170 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.26652v1 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: Deep hedging learns a hedging strategy by optimising a risk preference over a neural-network policy. The preference is fixed before training, so each new preference requires a new policy and, in actor-critic methods, a new critic. We propose distributional deep hedging, in which the distribution of the hedging profit and loss is learned through its quantiles and the risk preference is applied afterwards, as a weight on those quantiles. We characterise the preferences that admit this representation, which include expected shortfall and its mixtures, and show that the entropic utility is computed from the same quantiles. At the current policy, each of these preferences is bounded below by an expected utility with the same gradient. This bound reduces risk-sensitive hedging to a sequence of risk-neutral problems, from which we derive policy-search and actor-critic algorithms. In numerical experiments, the learned hedges approach references computed by dynamic programming, and a single distributional critic trained without a preference can serve preferences chosen after training.

  • Sources indicate that with a custom execution role, you define what StackSets can do in each account.
  • It has been revealed that to get started, choose Set execution role when you create a stack set in the CloudFormation console, or use the AWS CLI or AWS SDKs.

Recent findings suggest that AWS CloudFormation StackSets now supports custom execution roles for service-managed stack sets, which enables you to scope the permissions StackSets uses in each target AWS account. StackSets deploys the same infrastructure, such as networking and security settings, across thousands of accounts and Regions in one operation. With a custom execution role, you can also use nested stacks, macros, and transforms in service-managed stack sets, which allows you to deploy the reusable templates you use for individual stacks across your organization.

Sources indicate that with a custom execution role, you define what StackSets can do in each account. By default, service-managed stack sets use a role in each account that can provision any resource in a template without additional setup, and that default remains available. Now, you can provide a template that defines an IAM role, called the execution role, and StackSets creates it in each account before deploying. For example, a stack set that creates Amazon S3 buckets can use an execution role limited to CloudFormation and Amazon S3 permissions. When you enhancement the execution role template, StackSets updates the role in every account it deployed to.

It has been revealed that to get started, choose Set execution role when you create a stack set in the CloudFormation console, or use the AWS CLI or AWS SDKs. To learn more, visit the documentation and the AWS DevOps Blog. This feature is available at no additional charge in all commercial AWS Regions, the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions, and the China Regions. Refer to the AWS Region table for details.

VerifiQuant: Governance-by-Execution for Financial LLM Workflows

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (182 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.26649v1 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: Large language models embedded in financial workflows fail most dangerously by emitting confident, well-formatted but wrong numbers with no signal distinguishing them from correct ones. We argue that the central deployment problem is governability: a system must determine when a question supports a numeric answer and when it should instead clarify, intercept, or refuse. We present VerifiQuant, a governance-by-execution framework that packages financial logic into inference contracts and evaluates each query through an executable diagnostic funnel before deterministic computation. This separation makes computation, clarification, and refusal structured and auditable while keeping financial arithmetic outside the language model. Against matched retrieval-and-execution baselines, and within a declared contract library, the principal benefit is not higher accuracy on well-posed questions but safer behavior when an input does not justify a number. When it finds no applicable contract, it says so instead of guessing. Coverage sweeps and failure analysis put a price on this boundary: safety is bought with coverage rather than with accuracy, and residual failures remain attributable to specific runtime frontiers.

You send up to 500 usage lines in one request and get the cost back right away, without saving an estimate to your account. While workload estimates let you create and save an estimate in Pricing Calculator, GetUsageLinesEstimatedCost returns a cost on demand, directly in your own tools and workflows.

GetUsageLinesEstimatedCost is generally available at no additional charge in all AWS Regions, except the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions and the China Regions.

It has been revealed that you can use built-in profiling options that AWS Glue provides for common baseline statistics or provide your own Data Quality Definition Language (DQDL) ruleset with analyzers, rules, or both to hold every table in a database to the same quality standards. You have the flexibility to run evaluations once when you create the configuration or set up triggers, so evaluations run on a schedule or whenever table metadata changes, including every Apache Iceberg commit. After three runs on a table, AWS Glue Data Quality flags anomalous statistics that drift outside expected bounds, surfacing changes that no rule covers. Results are accessible through the existing AWS Glue Data Quality APIs, or you can opt-in to write them to Apache Iceberg tables in the AWS Glue Data Catalog or to Amazon S3.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • AWS Lambda now supports a batch size of up to 10,000 messages for Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queue event source mappings (ESMs) in provisioned mode, up from 10 messages previously.
  • Industry observers note that customers use SQS FIFO queues with Lambda to build event-driven applications that need strict message ordering and deduplication.
  • Recent findings suggest that this feature is available for SQS FIFO ESMs in provisioned mode in all AWS commercial Regions.

AWS Lambda now supports a batch size of up to 10,000 messages for Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queue event source mappings (ESMs) in provisioned mode, up from 10 messages previously. With larger batches, you can process high-volume, ordered workloads such as financial transactions, order processing, and inventory updates with fewer invocations and higher throughput. Lambda continues to preserve message ordering within each message group.

Industry observers note that customers use SQS FIFO queues with Lambda to build event-driven applications that need strict message ordering and deduplication. With provisioned mode for SQS ESMs, you can use throughput controls to set a minimum and maximum number of event pollers to meet strict performance requirements. Previously, provisioned mode customers who needed higher throughput for SQS FIFO queues were limited by the maximum batch size of 10 messages. This required them to scale out invocations or add custom buffering logic, which added operational overhead and cost. With this launch, you can set a batch size of up to 10,000 messages and a batching window of up to 300 seconds for FIFO queues, so you can process large volumes of ordered messages in fewer invocations without re-architecting your applications.

Recent findings suggest that this feature is available for SQS FIFO ESMs in provisioned mode in all AWS commercial Regions. You can configure the batch size and the batching window when you create fresh ESMs or update existing ESMs by using the Lambda console, AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, AWS CloudFormation, AWS CDK, or AWS SAM. You can also use coding assistants such as Kiro, Claude Code, or Codex with the Agent Toolkit for AWS. To learn more, visit the AWS Lambda Developer Guide and the AWS Lambda pricing.

It has been revealed that AWS Lambda now provides cost optimization recommendations for Event Functions in AWS Trusted Advisor. These recommendations identify on-demand functions where moving to Lambda Managed Instances (LMI) is estimated to reduce costs, and provide configuration guidance for running on LMI. With these recommendations, you can lower your Lambda costs by focusing your efforts on the functions with the greatest estimated savings.

In a recent development, LMI lets you run Lambda functions on Amazon EC2 instances while maintaining the operational simplicity of Lambda. With LMI, you can access specialized compute configurations and drive cost efficiency through EC2 pricing options such as Savings Aims and Reserved Instances, without managing infrastructure. Previously, to determine whether a function was a good fit for LMI, you had to analyze its invocation patterns, estimate LMI costs, and select the right instance type and memory-to-vCPU ratio yourself. This manual process added overhead and delayed savings. With this launch, Lambda automatically analyzes the invocation patterns, duration, and resource utilization of your high-volume Event Functions and recommends those where LMI is estimated to reduce costs. Estimates are based on a simulation of each function's invocation patterns, using public Lambda pricing and Amazon EC2 On-Demand pricing. Each recommendation includes the function ARN, the recommended EC2 instance type and memory-to-vCPU ratio, the estimated current cost, the estimated LMI cost, and the estimated savings. You can use the recommended configuration to run a function on LMI without sizing it yourself and realize cost savings sooner.

Sources indicate that these recommendations are available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Europe (Ireland), and Europe (Milan). Customers with eligible AWS Support intends can access them in the Trusted Advisor console alongside other cost optimization checks. To learn more, visit the AWS Lambda Developer Guide, the AWS Trusted Advisor User Guide, and the AWS Lambda pricing.

Sources indicate that builders using the latest AWS experience on the Paid plan can now receive spend limit alerts by text message (SMS), alongside existing email notifications. A spend limit sets the maximum monthly cost for a project. Notifications are sent as a project approaches its limit, and when a project reaches its limit, AWS automatically pauses it. SMS gives builders a second way to stay informed about their project costs.

Industry observers note that email alerts can go unnoticed when builders are away from their inbox, leaving little time to respond before a project is paused. SMS alerts close this gap with a text message when a project's actual costs reach 90% of its spend limit, so builders have time to act, such as raising the limit or stopping resources they don't need.

According to recent reports, to turn on SMS alerts, verify your mobile phone number in AWS Settings and turn on text alerts for spend limits. Text alerts are only sent to verified numbers, and you can opt out at any time. SMS alerts for spend limits are available at no additional charge for US phone numbers, including Puerto Rico, Guam, the US Virgin Islands, and American Samoa.

To learn more, see Create a spend limit in AWS Settings, the AWS Account Management Reference Guide, or Get started with AWS.

Amazon fights the Delivery Protection Act with homepage banner, in-app pop-up

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (531 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In an unprecedented move, Amazon is using its app and website to try to convince shoppers to not support a New York City bill.
  • In a recent development, I also saw a smaller version of the notice on an order confirmation page on Amazon’s website.
  • Amazon is referring to Introduction 0518-2026 ( 518), also known as the Delivery Protection Act.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In an unprecedented move, Amazon is using its app and website to try to convince shoppers to not support a New York City bill.

In a recent development, I also saw a smaller version of the notice on an order confirmation page on Amazon’s website. The message is delivered as a pop-up for customers of the Amazon app, Bloomberg reported. Amazon hasn’t specified whether the messaging targets NYC residents based on addresses saved in their Amazon account or uses other techniques, such as device location services, but I only see the banner if I’m logged in to Amazon.

Amazon is referring to Introduction 0518-2026 ( 518), also known as the Delivery Protection Act. If passed, it would require Amazon to directly employ the third-party delivery contractors that it uses.

Clicking on “Act now” on Amazon’s homepage or in the app brings up a page that gives shoppers a way to contact their NYC Council member and further states:.

Right now, Amazon works with a network of small delivery businesses that are deeply embedded in your communities. If this legislation passes, we’d no longer be able to work with them, and we’d be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city. That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees.

Industry observers note that it’s not unusual for Amazon to take a stance on political matters, and it has publicly opposed the Delivery Protection Act since April. What is upcoming is Amazon using its online marketplace to push a political view. It’s uncommon to see a pop-up about legislation when visiting a shopping website.

The messaging suggests that Amazon is concerned about the potential impact the proposed law would have on its costs. Besides Amazon, the bill targets any organization with last-mile delivery facilities in NYC, like FedEx and DoorDash.

It also raises questions about the potential impact on shoppers should Amazon expand its use of its e-commerce platform for additional political messaging. The pop-up debuted today impacts only NYC residents but sets a precedent for Amazon to sway political views on other issues. Amazon has made similar moves internally, including reportedly using an app for its employees to campaign against unionizing. But the newly introduced pop-up shows Amazon extending that strategy directly to its owners.

Given Amazon’s considerable influence in commerce, other companies could copy its actions. Uber and Lyft have previously done so, CNBC reports.

Industry observers note that finally, there’s the question of whether Amazon is fairly depicting the situations surrounding the bill. Notable supporters of the Delivery Protection Act include NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the Amazon division of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters. Using a platform with massive reach to communicate only one side of an ongoing debate could lead to misinformation and a skewed public perception.

Sources indicate that the Delivery Protection Act is currently stalled in the City Council’s Committee on Consumer and Worker Protection. The last hearing on the bill was in April. A committee vote on whether to advance the act to the full City Council hasn’t been set.
