Recent findings suggest that at 16 years old, Henrijs Dandzbergs is too young to vote. Or drink. Or smoke. Or drive unsupervised. But he’s not too young to win half a million dollars for his AI-guided-missile startup.

It has been revealed that in September, Dandzbergs, who was born in Latvia, was admitted to Y Combinator’s fall 2026 cohort. The startup accelerator counts companies like Airbnb, Stripe, DoorDash, and Reddit among its alumni; Dandzbergs is likely the youngest solo founder in its vaunted history.

According to recent reports, his startup, Polemos Industries, is attempting to develop a upcoming class of precision-guided missile that can be easily and cheaply manufactured, can be fired from portable launchers, and can resist jamming attempts. “I think missiles are the coolest thing,” Dandzbergs tells WIRED. “A lot of people that have found success in engineering early on have had a passion for blowing stuff up.”.

Industry observers note that in conversation, Dandzbergs is poised and articulate. He talks about “attacking hard problems,” breaking things down to “first principles,” and how the Ukraine conflict has forever altered the theater of war—a personal fixation, given his country's proximity to Russia. He projects an unassailable confidence in his own abilities.

Recent findings suggest that “He’s a pretty exceptional person,” says Harj Taggar, a YC partner assigned to mentor Dandzbergs. “I’m still somewhat in disbelief that we’re talking about a 16-year-old.”.

Industry observers note that dandzbergs has resolved to apply these unusual talents to figuring out how to optimize targeted killing. His startup’s guiding ambition, according to its investor one-pager, is to bring down the “cost per kill.”.

As a young(er) kid, Dandzbergs was rarely in one place for long; his family moved between Latvia, Indonesia, Australia, and Spain. His surfer father, part owner of an insurance organization, likes to go wherever he might find the raddest waves.

Early in his schooling, which mostly took place online, Dandzbergs demonstrated a clear talent for science and math. His room started to look like a lab, littered with schematics, robotics, Raspberry Pis, and 3D-printed components.

In a recent development, when Covid struck, Dandzbergs’ family returned to Latvia. His parents enrolled him in Astra Nova, an Elon Musk–linked school where students undergo an experimental curriculum built around lateral thinking and problem-solving instead of rote memorization. Dandzbergs took a class taught by a NASA employee and became fascinated by aerospace engineering. His lab creations became ever more elaborate: a bionic arm, a thermal control system for a model rocket, sensors for a self-flying drone.

According to recent reports, around this time, Russia invaded Ukraine. In Latvia, Dandzbergs started to see military jets overhead, and stray missiles were intercepted at the Russian border. With the sovereignty of Eastern European nations under threat, new defense startups began to pop up across the region. Dandzbergs wanted in.

“A patriotic intention to protect my country, European countries, and Ukrainian and American soldiers, and understanding the future of autonomous warfare—that’s my drive,” he says.

To stretch his technical skills, Dandzbergs started to take part in hackathons, where software and hardware engineers compete to develop the most sophisticated prototype from scratch.

In April of this year, he flew to London to take part in a hackathon held by Unicorn Mafia, an invitation-only group of developers. The prize included $10,000 in cash, a plane ticket to San Francisco, and free legal assistance with O-1 visa applications to stay in the US.

Less than 48 hours later, Dandzbergs and his two teammates, Aleksandrs Tihenko and Kai Yang, had built an AI system that could design hardware circuit boards from natural language prompts, much like how a software engineer might use AI to generate code. Though his teammates are both a few years older, Dandzbergs pushed for them to include even more intricate features in the prototype. “It was amazing,” claims Tihenko. “The imagination of Henrijs in the hardware space is just crazy.”.

Industry observers note that seeing that they stood no chance of beating Dandzbergs’ group and other front-runners, teams started to drop out of the competition, according to Fergus McKenzie-Wilson, Unicorn Mafia’s director and one of the hackathon judges. “What they built was incredibly impressive,” he claims. “No one had ever seen that before.”.

Recent findings suggest that when the organizers crowned Dandzbergs’ team victorious, somebody handed him the mic. “I’m 16 years old,” he mentioned.

The week after the hackathon, Dandzbergs and his teammates pitched their circuit board concept to YC. They won a place in the summer program, but Dandzbergs wavered over whether he should drop out of high school. The trio also sparred over whether the startup should focus on applying the technology to the defense sector, Dandzbergs’ primary area of interest. Dandzbergs ended up pulling out of the partnership. “It was hard,” says Tihenko. “But ultimately we just settled that the best decision for the firm would be to part ways and focus on different things.”.

By the summer, Danzbergs was set on building a defense startup and reapplied to YC on his own. He had spotted a gap in the market, he claimed, for AI-guided missiles that were more precise and could carry bigger warheads than the drones deployed widely in Ukraine. His products, he added, would be cheaper and easier to manufacture than hulking great rocket systems.

YC initially tried to steer him away. Dandzbergs was promising a lot of everything, all at once. It wasn’t clear whether his idea could work or whether pulling out of school was the right thing for him to do. “There’s a paternal element to it,” says Taggar. “You don’t want to be screwing up people's lives—and working on a startup is a pretty serious thing.”.

Industry observers note that dandzbergs is up against a fleet of defense companies—from Anduril to CoAspire to Leidos—aiming to develop cheaper, mass-producible missiles. The more sophisticated the guidance system, the more difficult that task becomes.

It has been revealed that “You can build a cheap missile that doesn’t go very far. You can build a cheap missile that doesn’t carry much of a payload. You can build a cheap missile that has a low reliability rate,” claims Tom Karako, director of the Missile Defense Project and senior fellow at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. “There are trade-offs.”.

But Dandzbergs wasn’t going to be dissuaded, and YC figured that somebody else would probably invest in his idea. The incubator invited him to join its fall program. “Big picture, you never know if these things are possible or not,” states Taggar. “Is it a non-zero-percent chance that it could be possible? That’s frankly the threshold, especially if it’s a really big [idea].”.

So far, according to Dandzbergs, Polemos Industries has developed the software system that will guide its missiles and has begun to hammer out elements of the hardware design. By the time the YC program finishes in December, he hopes to be able to showcase a prototype missile.

If he does ultimately succeed, though, Dandzbergs will need to confront an assortment of hairy ethical quandaries. Who should have access to these new missiles? What if a technical error were to result in friendly fire? Can he make peace with his technology being used to end somebody’s life?

Dandzbergs claims that he has come to terms with these issues. He notes he takes solace in the belief that his motivations are pure: to protect the US and its European allies.

By his logic, autonomous weapons are an inevitable part of the future, so he might as well be the one who builds them. “I choose not to shy away from the emergence of modern conflict as a global issue. I simply don’t have a lot of respect for people that do,” he claims. “I want to be part of it. I want to move with the future of warfare.”.

But others who have found themselves in a similar position say it’s difficult to know in advance how somebody will deal with the knowledge that their invention has killed people.

McKenzie-Wilson, the Unicorn Mafia director, introduced a drone startup in his early twenties. Initially, he had meant for the drones to evacuate wounded soldiers, but after a missile organization invested, his startup retooled its technology to drop payloads too. He left around the same time.

“I don’t think I was emotionally mature enough,” he claims. “[Dandzbergs] will realize at some point. He’ll either have an issue with it or he won’t.”.

Polemos Industries confirmed itself publicly on November 5 with a glossy social media video. Set to the ticking of a clock, it featured a set of four missiles fired into the sky from ground launchers, then blowing a convoy of four military vehicles to smithereens.

It has been revealed that the video climbed to the top of the trending page on X. In the responses, a couple of people tagged Palmer Luckey, cofounder of Anduril, who was 19 when he started his first company. “Coming for him,” Dandzbergs responded.

Dandzbergs recognizes that people are likely to dismiss him for his age. But he considers youth one of his biggest advantages. “Please don’t say I’m sacrificing my childhood,” he claims. “This is the childhood I dreamed of.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it’s been said that us gadget enthusiasts who review tech for a living can accumulate a lot of debris. Boxes of adapters, old cables, and other device detritus can hang around longer than we probably need them, but we hang on to them just in case we need exactly that port or cord length someday. You never know.

No one’s needed a VGA-to-HDMI adapter for a while, but you never know — better to be prepared in case, why not?

Recent findings suggest that still, I could stand to do a little organizing, especially going into the holiday shopping season. I’m trying to get rid of whatever I don’t need, and my collection of dongles, adapters, and cables is long overdue for a closer look.

Also: Why your USB-C cables look alike, but work differently – and how to tell them apart.

Before I send everything willy-nilly to my local recycling center, where the seagulls can pick them over, there are a few essentials I should keep. Here’s what’s still useful and why, even if they’re old or functionally obsolete.

The experts told us that USB-C connectivity would make everything better by giving you one cable and charger for everything. But you’d be surprised how many gadgets with a USB-C port won’t charge when a USB-C-to-USB-C cable is attached to a USB-C charger. That issue often occurs because the gadgets lack the circuitry to activate the charger.

Also: Your headphones’ USB-C port has 4 hidden features – but you need the right cable.

The biggest clue to the problem is that the item ships with a USB-A-to-USB-C cable. Another indicator that something’s wrong is that nothing happens when you connect the device to the charging cable for your smartphone.

Industry observers note that this issue explains why it’s still a good idea to keep a trusty USB-A-to-USB-C cable around. Oh, and a charger that can accept it.

Industry observers note that again, this is a port that won’t die. Many cheaper devices still use this port (for example, it’s used regularly by cheap power banks from Temu and eBay).

While the connection is annoying, old, and prone to breakage, having a USB-A-to-microUSB charge cable is still a good idea.

In a recent development, as our reliance on USB-enabled power increases, the power cord is slowly but surely vanishing. But don’t throw away all your old cords. I suggest keeping one C7 (two-pin, often called a “figure of eight”) and one three-pin earthed C13.

C13 power cord connector (left) and C8 (right).

According to recent reports, wireless might be crucial today, but cabled connections still have their place. Just the other day, I needed an Ethernet cable to connect to a security camera during setup, and I then used the same cable to connect the camera’s base station to the router.

Also: The top-selling cords, cables, and chargers readers bought this year (including a cheap favorite).

It has been revealed that moral of the story? Keep a few Ethernet cables of varying lengths (one, three, and six feet) handy. If you’re feeling particularly ambitious, grab a reel of cable, some connectors, and an RJ45 crimping tool to make your own. It’s a strangely satisfying process.

While USB chargers have largely replaced DC chargers, there’s still a place for these older devices for cordless handsets, routers, and more.

If you don’t want a drawer full of mismatched chargers, pick up a universal device.

My Mac has an SD card reader, but no microSD slot, Ethernet port, or USB-A port. That’s why I always keep a USB dock around; it’s the Swiss Army Knife of ports. Over the years, I’ve collected a small collection of docks, and while I’m not keeping all of them, I’ll keep a couple “just in case.”.

It has been revealed that there are also some things you can add to your tech gear utility belt. These items are useful beyond their size and cost, including:.

Recent findings suggest that these USB-C boost modules are great for converting non-USB devices into USB. All you need is a bit of know-how.

My power meter has seen a lot of action, but it still works.

Of course, I’m still haunted by the vague, nagging fear that the moment I get rid of a cable or adapter, some bizarre, one-in-a-million situation will arise in which I need it. But you know what? If Aunt Jackie’s neighbor’s cat sitter comes a-knocking, they’re on their own.

Recent findings suggest that the gym bro in your life never stops moving. Monday: chest. Tuesday: back. Wednesday: leg day. Plus, real ones never forget about cardio. With that kind of split, muscle recovery is a nonnegotiable. The Theragun Pro Plus is the elite massage gun for when his hammies are crying louder than his “Get Swole” playlist blaring through the speakers. Along with percussive therapy, it offers vibrations, heat, and near-infrared LED light therapies to optimize muscle recovery and pain relief. It comes with seven attachments, 150 minutes of battery life, and Bluetooth connectivity for guided routines in the Therabody app.

Check out our guide to the Best Massage Guns for more muscle-recovery gift ideas.

Real gym bros don’t read screens on their fitness trackers to get minute-by-minute, tiny progress notes. That makes the Whoop MG the bro-iest fitness tracker; its proprietary algorithm doesn’t measure teensy metrics like step count. The Whoop doesn’t care if you stand up every hour! Instead, “Strain” is a scale that runs from 1 to 21 based on the Borg rating of perceived exertion. Strain takes into account your previous day’s recovery, so the score you earn from day to day—even from the same activities—will be different.

In a recent development, last year, Whoop introduced latest features like Healthspan, Pace of Aging, and other cardiac features with the Whoop MG and the Whoop Life membership. These help a bro monitor more than just his muscle growth—after all, even gym bros need a break from powerlifting every day.—Adrienne So.

Recent findings suggest that this is for the gym bro who talks about macros to the extent that I talk about The Real Housewives (hint: it’s a lot). Transparent Labs is one of the few supplement brands that tests both ingredients and finished products for heavy metals and then posts the results online.

The Grass-Fed Whey Protein Isolate is sourced from hormone-free cows and skips dyes and artificial sweeteners. Each serving delivers 28 grams of protein, but if your broski’s deep in a bulking era, the Mass Gainer may be more his speed. It comes with 50 grams of protein and 100 grams of carbs, and Consumer Reports has vetted the Sweet Vanilla flavor for daily consumption.

For other protein powder recommendations, check out some of our other tested favorites.

Rule number one: a gym bro can never have too many shaker bottles. It’s a gym essential and the perfect gift when you don’t know too much about your homie. The BlenderBottle Classic is the OG of shaker bottles: It features measurement markings, a spout guard to prevent spills, and a carry loop for keeping grubby hands off the mouthpiece (or clipping on keys). Its rounded base and BlenderBall whisk crush clumps, so every sip is smooth(ish), depending on the protein powder, of course. It’s BPA- and phthalate-free, dishwasher-safe, and available in three sizes (20, 28, and 45 ounces).

Industry observers note that creatine won’t turn you into the Rock overnight, but when paired with regular weightlifting and a nutritious diet, it can help preserve strength and lean body mass. (But your gym bro probably already knows this.) There are several versions of creatine out there, but it’s best to stick to monohydrate; it’s the most studied, the most reliable, and usually the most affordable. Thorne’s flavorless powder is perfect for blending into smoothies or mixing with water before a workout.

Pro tip: When they hit you with a “Bro, I’m looking swole lately” after three days on creatine, maybe don’t mention it’s mostly water weight. Let them have this one.

According to recent reports, body scales—like dietary supplements—should be a request, not a surprise; I would only gift one if they’ve explicitly mentioned they want one. Nevertheless, this scale is for the gym rat who tracks macros in their sleep. If they’re logging every rep, meal, and REM cycle, they’ll love the Runstar FG2015 Smart Scale. Unlike a standard foot-only scale, this one has a retractable handle with electrodes that scan your whole body and analyze muscle mass, water weight, and visceral fat. Does the average person need that level of detail? No, but if they’re bodybuilding, bulking, or just like to boast about their body fat percentage down to the decimal, it’s a total game-changer.

For more recommendations, we weighed in on other smart scales in this guide.

Real gym bros are not afraid to stretch. The Manduka ProLite is my personal favorite yoga mat because it’s versatile enough for mobility work, hot mat Pilates, and strength training. The closed-cell PVC surface keeps out sweat, bacteria, and whatever else’s festering on the gym floor. It’s dense enough to cushion knees without feeling squishy and is also latex- and phthalate-free. It’s an awesome addition to their home gym (because you know they have one).

Find more yoga mat options here.

In a recent development, the Hydro Flask is the ultimate gift for a gym lover. Built like a dumbbell, it can survive drops, dents, and tosses into any gym bag or back seat. It keeps water cold for hours and comes in a ton of sizes and colors. Order directly from the site to customize the lid, strap, and bottle; you can also engrave their name so no one accidentally walks off with their bottle again.

For more recommendations, check out our guide to the Best Reusable Water Bottles.

A real gym bro makes getting to the gym part of the fitness routine. The XP4 750 is one of the most popular options on the market. It folds in half for easy storage and fits a range of rider heights and sizes. It has an upgraded motor from the original, but Quad Squad bros know to turn it off and pedal this 71-pound beast with pure leg strength for a real workout. —Harry Rabinowitz.

Some of our favorite gym workout headphones, the BlueAnt Pump X, have a pretty remarkable standout feature. You can swap out the regular ear pads for cooling gel ear pads, which you can store in the fridge when you’re not using them. If your bro has ever found that keeping noise-canceling headphones on his head while he concentrates on his form makes him feel too sweaty, these are worth a shot. They work remarkably well, even if the condiment drawer in the fridge is a weird place to store workout equipment. —Adrienne So.

Yes, your bro has been lifting in Chuck Taylors for his whole life, and they work fine. But if he needs an upgrade, may we suggest R.A.D. shoes, which are designed for gym, HIIT, CrossFit, and hybrid workouts and are soft enough to run on the treadmill. The rubber rand protects his feet for rope exercises, and like his beloved Chucks, the sole is flat for stabilization during lifting and drills like box jumps. Also, they look the best. 💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that the biggest video game ever has turned out to be one of the very best.
  • Recent findings suggest that I’ve spent a few hours in the game, and one thing becomes clear right away: This game is a slow burn.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hey, maybe don’t just immediately go to the strip club. Look, I know that’s what you want to do right away when you start Grand Theft Auto VI. This is a GTA game after all—that sort of outlet for titillation is a common theme in this franchise. But going straight to the good stuff isn’t the best way to play this game.

It has been revealed that the biggest video game ever has turned out to be one of the very best. With near-universally perfect review scores, GTA VI has emerged as an absolute behemoth that has lived up to 13 years of hype.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve spent a few hours in the game, and one thing becomes clear right away: This game is a slow burn. The GTA franchise has always been high-octane, arcade-style, prioritizing hyperviolence and exaggerated physics that let your character go wild in the digital sandbox. But the latest installation is much more reserved. Vehicles and player movements feel heavier. The characters have deeper, more emotional backstories and motivations. The world has more interactivity and reacts to your actions in much more varied ways.

It has been revealed that it evokes a play style that feels very much in common with Rockstar’s previous title, Red Dead Redemption 2. It was a Western that made the player feel the friction of an often slow, plodding life that didn’t shy away from simulating all the chores of a horse-bound cowboy in the 1800s. GTA VI, set in the modern era, is faster-paced but still carries that intentionality to slow the player down.

It has been revealed that that manifests in ways that might feel like busywork. Instead of having access to all your weapons and outfits, you have to make space for the things you want to bring with you and store everything else in the back of your car. You have to call someone to fix your car and wait for them to arrive. Yeah, you have to paint your house and buy your girlfriend flowers. Get used to it. This can sometimes feel like a chore, but it slows the player down to give them time to examine the world around them.

It has been revealed that once you start looking around and really take everything in, the level of detail is truly unique. Leonida—GTA VI’s mirror version of Miami, Florida—is so varied and splendid it is almost overwhelming. After the game’s on-the-rails introductory missions open up into the first opportunity for an open-world sojourn, the sheer scale of this world becomes apparent. Zooming out on the map and seeing the vast expanse of unexplored territory is dizzying.

There is just so much Leonida, and none of it feels sparse or unfinished. Every place, person, animal, and environmental asset feels fully fleshed out. Driving down the road, with other cars zooming past, is photorealistic enough to look nearly like real dash-cam footage. This game, as I have muttered to myself over and over again while playing, “is simply insane.”.

It has been revealed that if you’ve followed the GTA VI saga, this likely won’t surprise you. Developer Rockstar and its parent firm Take-Two have spent around a billion dollars to develop the game. It’s taken 13 years. The company even delayed the game multiple times to make sure it was polished.

There is massive hype, and at this point I’d say what Rockstar has achieved here has surpassed that hype. The game is likely to be the pinnacle of this era of video games, the final grand blockbuster achieved without the use of generative AI.

Sources indicate that I’ve been playing GTA games for a long time. I’ll probably be playing this one for the rest of my life. Like me, you’re probably very excited to dive into this gigantic world. The best way to do that is not to try to see it all at once. Pace yourself. Look out for the small moments, as they may lead to something more profound than you’re expecting. Slow down, and you can really feel how the world reacts.

Industry observers note that nothing else like this game exists. And there probably won’t be for a very long time. Might as well make it last.

#23907. El Niño Is Driving a Record Marine Heat Wave Off the California Coast

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (808 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

El Niño Is Driving a Record Marine Heat Wave Off the California Coast

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (808 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, for the past 20 years, Daniel Rudnick has been collecting data from below the ocean’s surface.
  • The oceanographer helps to pilot small underwater drones known as gliders that dive thousands of feet below the surface and crawl their way back up, collecting data on salinity, temperature, and other metrics.
  • A color-coded chart showing temperature anomalies at different depths in the ocean—red for hotter, blue for colder—had to be readjusted because the red shades weren’t intense enough to accurately reflect just how hot things are, even hundreds of meters below the surface.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, for the past 20 years, Daniel Rudnick has been collecting data from below the ocean’s surface. He’s never seen anything like what’s been coming back for the past few months, as a super El Niño fuels record heat off the California coast. The marine heat wave is affecting wildlife and helping to juice the record-setting storms hitting the state at the start of the rainy season.

The oceanographer helps to pilot small underwater drones known as gliders that dive thousands of feet below the surface and crawl their way back up, collecting data on salinity, temperature, and other metrics.

A color-coded chart showing temperature anomalies at different depths in the ocean—red for hotter, blue for colder—had to be readjusted because the red shades weren’t intense enough to accurately reflect just how hot things are, even hundreds of meters below the surface. Steric height—changes to sea levels driven by heat rather than melting ice—has reached the highest levels Rudnick has ever seen.

“I looked back at our data to make sure that I'm not making a mistake and it's correct—and it is,” Rudnick, who works at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography at UC San Diego, claims.

In Monterey Bay, a station recorded a temperature of 64.72 degrees Fahrenheit (18.18 degrees Celsius) at a depth of 200 feet below the water’s surface in late October, breaking previous records. Other data highlights even hotter water in San Diego at the same depth: 77 degrees Fahrenheit, an anomaly of 21.3 degrees Fahrenheit above normal.

El Niño “is the biggest source of climate variability” off the California coast, Rudnick indicates. The climate phenomenon is characterized by hotter-than-normal water in the eastern tropical Pacific and affects weather and oceans around the globe. His gliders have captured temperature anomalies across other events, including intense heat during the 2015–2016 super El Niño. But this year’s El Niño is shaping up to be the strongest on record, and its impacts are equally supersized.

“It’s fair to say it’s off the charts,” he notes.

This year’s El Niño is adding heat to an already-simmering ocean. Since January 2025, coastal California waters have been hit by a massive heat wave, with temperatures in some places reaching 8 degrees Fahrenheit above average in August. Add in human-caused climate change—oceans off Southern California have warmed 1.8 degrees Fahrenheit since the 1970s alone—and it makes for unprecedented conditions now.

Industry observers note that “This is a bunch of things that have had to come together to make this even physically possible,” Daniel Swain, a climate scientist at the University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources, says. “And even then, it's kind of astonishing.”.

It has been revealed that rudnick agrees. “The heat we get from El Niño stacking on top of the heat we already have, that’s the thing that makes this most unusual,” he says.

Industry observers note that part of what’s driving the higher ocean temperatures and sea levels off California are what’s known as Kelvin waves. These slow, large waves transport warm water from west to east across the Pacific. They in turn push down the ocean’s thermocline, a transition layer into the deeper ocean where temperatures begin to decrease rapidly.

“It isn't like there's some heater in the deep ocean suddenly,” Swain says. “It's just that we've turned off the air conditioner and we're allowing the surface waters to warm.”.

It has been revealed that kelvin waves can also help to raise sea levels along the California coast by “keeping the water from moving physically offshore,” Swain says. While Kelvin waves are imperceptible to the average person, their impacts aren’t.

Californians have been living through several weeks of intense coastal flooding and big waves enhanced by these higher sea levels. San Francisco and the surrounding area are under a coastal flood advisory through Friday morning, and waves have reached over 30 feet (9 meters) in height and even set off seismographs. (Another storm is set to hit the Bay Area this weekend.) It’s also contributing to heavier rainfall, with locations from San Francisco to Burbank setting hourly rainfall records in recent days.

But the warmer water itself is also contributing to this temporary sea level rise, thanks to simple physics: Warmer water takes up more space, helping push up sea levels.

The warm water is driving weather even more unprecedented than the intense storms. On Tuesday, two rare twin waterspouts formed over San Francisco Bay, the result of cold storm air moving over unusually warm waters. These phenomena are generally seen off the coast of Florida or the Mediterranean—not in the usually frigid waters of the Pacific.

Sources indicate that “The air temperatures are somewhat winter-like right now, but the water ain't,” Swain says. “It’s an indicator that things aren’t as they usually are in this part of the world.”.

The deliciously vibrant OLED display is brighter and bigger than in the past, and if you opt for the nano-texture screen, it becomes the ultimate outdoor tablet. It might be a bit too expensive for a tablet of its size, but it just might be the ultimate travel companion for the right person.

Recent findings suggest that this Sonos speaker is built different, quite literally. It’s made specifically with Dolby Atmos spatial audio in mind, with six speaker drivers pointed in multiple directions to spread out sound like no other home speaker can. Outside of Atmos, it’s an excellent stereo speaker that sounds crisp and detailed, and can connect with Sonos soundbars to make a full surround sound setup. —Harry Rabinowitz.

It has been revealed that you know what they say: If it ain't broke, don't fix it. The Logitech MX Master 3S has long been the most popular productivity mouse you can buy, so expectations for its successor were high. Thankfully, the MX Master 4 (9/10, WIRED Recommends) delivers without rocking the boat too much. There's now haptic support in the thumb rest, and you can press here to activate the virtual Actions Ring. You can customize the ring in the Logi Options+ app to launch apps, open websites, insert symbols, or even type text—the options are nearly endless.

It has been revealed that it might not be worth upgrading from the MX Master 3 or 3S, especially since the polling rate hasn't changed, but the MX Master 4 has taken the reins as the go-to wireless mouse for serious office workers. If you know someone who would appreciate a mouse that not only offers great ergonomic support but also feels extremely high-quality in the hand, look no further.

For more ideas for home office products that make great gifts, check out our comprehensive guide to the Best Work-from-Home Gear.

In a recent development, whether it's the Rabbit R1 or Humane Pin, AI hardware has been a significant flop so far. But this year, we finally started to see devices that are actually interesting and potentially useful. WIRED contributor Christopher Null tried out all the fresh product category of AI notetaking devices, which can dictate, record, summarize, and translate seamlessly using large language models. Pocket was among the top recommendations. It magnetically attaches to the back of your phone and can even record phone calls without needing to keep it on speakerphone. Many AI notetakers require a paid subscription, while Pocket offers a substantial free option and only requires Pocket Pro as an upgrade for unlimited history.

With all the earbuds we review, you might think our audio experts are above something as common as AirPods. But Apple really nailed it this year with the AirPods Pro 3 (9/10, WIRED Recommends). It's been almost three years since Apple updated its noise-canceling earbuds, and the latest model adds a fresh ear tip design, supports real-time translation, and delivers vastly improved noise canceling and longer battery life. According to our testers, the earbuds last up to eight hours with noise canceling on, enough for more than a full day of work. All that makes this pair the best AirPods ever made.

In a recent development, goPro has a latest premium camera, and it's one of the most expensive action cameras you can buy. But our camera expert and outdoors enthusiast, Scott Gilbertson, says it's totally worth it. The new model, the GoPro Mission 1 Pro, has a larger 1-inch sensor than the Hero models, letting it shoot up to 8K at 60 fps. That might sound like overkill, but 8K lets you crop and zoom in on what you capture on your adventures while exporting to 4K without a big hit to image quality (unless you're fortunate enough to own an 8K TV). Scott also praises the new slow-motion mode, shooting up to 4K at 240 fps—even when zoomed in. The older GoPro Hero 13 Black is still a great option if you want to save some money, but the Mission 1 Pro's upgrade in image quality is noteworthy for a camera this small.

Industry observers note that the best espresso machines cost well over $1,000 and take up your entire kitchen counter. They aren't exactly very “giftable.” The Breville Bambino challenges that assumption. It's only $300, yet it has many of the same features as more expensive machines, such as a thermoblock for instant heating. Of course, as a smaller, budget option, it's missing some things, such as automatic milk frothing. But according to former WIRED reviewer, Matthew Korfhage, pairing the Bambino with a solid grinder gives you “beautiful cups with counter space to spare.” Who wouldn't want that?

Sources indicate that smart Play is Lego's next big move into adding some serious tech into its classic brick-building. Despite looking like standard Legos, each Smart Brick has a custom chip, light array, speaker, and a variety of sensors. You can probably imagine how all this tech plays out in a set as immersive as the Star Wars Throne Room Duel. If you want to experience the latest in the world of Lego, it doesn't get more cutting-edge than this (even if our reviewer found that the tech took some of the magic away).

#23904. Regular Tech Bros Are Worried About Honeypots

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1170 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Regular Tech Bros Are Worried About Honeypots

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1170 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When the founder of a cybersecurity firm hired Blaine Anderson as a matchmaker, it wasn’t just because the man was lonely.
  • In a recent development, the cybersecurity founder isn’t the only one.
  • “Even if you're not a CEO or at a substantial tech giant, these fears have trickled down to just regular professionals,” Simone Grossman, a Brooklyn-based matchmaker, tells WIRED.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When the founder of a cybersecurity firm hired Blaine Anderson as a matchmaker, it wasn’t just because the man was lonely. It was also, Anderson indicates, because he was “super worried about spies.”.

In a recent development, the cybersecurity founder isn’t the only one. As Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged asset of China’s Ministry of State Security dominates headlines and AI companies reportedly warn employees against “honeypots,” matchmakers say that more men with pretty normal lives are worried that their dates may have ulterior motives: accessing corporate secrets.

“Even if you're not a CEO or at a substantial tech giant, these fears have trickled down to just regular professionals,” Simone Grossman, a Brooklyn-based matchmaker, tells WIRED.

One tech worker, who requested anonymity in order to speak candidly, claims he considers himself “highly selective” about the people he interacts with face-to-face.

Sources indicate that “Even though I could vet you from looking you up online, I can't help but still be a tad dubious,” he tells WIRED. On a scale from zero to 10, with 10 being the most anxious about espionage, he puts himself at a seven.

Even though the vast majority of tech employees likely won’t be targeted for romantic espionage, matchmakers say more clients have lately expressed concerns about women exploiting them for their corporate secrets. One Palantir employee told Andersen he wouldn’t date anyone who was a Chinese or Russian national. The anxiety has even become a marketing opportunity: One firm is pitching its latest line of AI executive girlfriends as a “zero espionage” alternative to human dating.

Industry observers note that the concern isn’t entirely without basis. Some companies hire consultants to advise executives and lower-level employees with access to sensitive information on security risks, including the possibility of honeypots. Several of these consultants tell WIRED that raising the subject can be awkward.

“This one is always a very difficult message to deliver—to explain to, say, very sensitive engineers that maybe they're getting a lot of email attention because of their job,” states Isaac Stone Fish, founder and chief executive of the business intelligence firm Strategy Risks, “as opposed to the charm and force of their personality.”.

Amy Andersen, founder of Silicon Valley matchmaking company Linx Dating (and no relation to Blaine Anderson), claims that for clients concerned about their romantic partners’ intentions, she offers background checks, personal vetting, and NDAs. The security features are part of her “bespoke” packages that range anywhere from $75,000 to more than $500,000 for the “Founders Level.”.

Sources indicate that fear of romantic espionage is just the latest manifestation of growing distrust in the dating world. Shannon Lundgren, a matchmaker who has worked in San Francisco for 15 years, says that while she hasn’t necessarily heard more concerns about honeypots, she has noticed heightened skepticism around dating in general, as well as growing concerns about privacy.

The anxiety is particularly acute among AI workers, whose net worths—and therefore their perceived romantic desirability—are on the rise.

“If you're somebody who is a little bit shy or who is maybe a very stereotypical engineer type, to suddenly have your market value in the dating world change so drastically—you're already suspicious,” Grossman says.

To be worried about corporate espionage on top of all that, she notes, is “a mind fuck.”.

Honeypots and their state or corporate sponsors often look for “signs of vulnerability, such as an unhappy marriage, or someone seeking “excitement or adventure,” says Ira Winkler, a security consultant and the chief information security officer in residence at identity protection tech giant Cloaked. Lonely people are opportune targets, regardless of marriage or relationship status.

The advice security experts give is somewhat obvious: If it seems too good to be true, it probably is.

“Really, if a beautiful woman approaches you, you know it's not for your personality,” Winkler tells his clients.

Recent findings suggest that when tech workers do think of honeypots, they may gravitate toward the stereotype of a beautiful stranger who seduces someone at a bar and then extracts tech giant secrets. “Any time one of us would take a trip to Asia, someone would always make a comment about getting a foreign girlfriend, or future wife, etc.,” one tech worker tells WIRED about his experience at a majority-male workplace. “We'd joke about them meeting a spy, but nobody really considered that seriously. Mostly they were just thinking of sex.”.

In a recent development, that setup is largely a misconception. In reality, according to Greg Rinckey, founding partner of the legal services and consulting firm Tully Rinckey, most honeypot victims are groomed over time. “We’re talking sometimes months, could be years, where they're fostering that relationship,” he notes. Rinckey compares it to scammers trying to keep victims on the phone: The longer someone talks to another person and feels they know them, the more likely they are to trust them with sensitive information.

Sources indicate that catherine Marinis-Yaqub, a principal at the crisis and security consulting group Control Risks, tells WIRED that when people imagine the beautiful stranger at a bar, they may miss more likely scenarios, like an unexpected guest at a business meeting, a savvy networker at an industry conference, or a flirt at someone’s favorite coffee shop. Jensen Huang met Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese asset, for example, through a mutual business associate (who, according to The Wall Street Journal, also happened to be Alice’s husband).

For the man too scared of spies to make contact with a human romantic partner, there’s always artificial intelligence.

In a recent development, on Tuesday, in the wake of the Huang scandal, AI-relationship platform Joi AI released a suite of "zero espionage" Executive Girlfriends. Brand director Julie Levin describes Joi AI as a “safe space” for exploration, where people can exchange NSFW texts, images, and videos with AI companions without judgment or rejection.

It made sense, she says, to extend that sense of security to honeypot-phobia.

“If they have some business secrets they don't want to share on a date or they feel nervous discussing with real people,” Levin says, “they can discuss them comfortably with their AIs.” (Levin assures WIRED that Joi AI employs several layers of security and that all of the data is anonymized.).

High-profile executives are among those most at risk of honeypots, claims Winkler, the security consultant. They can also be some of the hardest to protect.

“It's really hard to influence somebody who's in control of the tech giant and just happens to be a sleazebag,” Winkler notes.

It’s particularly difficult, says Rinckey, when bosses think they’re the smartest person in the room and consider themselves immune to manipulation. It’s also not easy, he says, to be in the position of challenging an executive.

Recent findings suggest that “Cocky, arrogant, and boisterous” chief executives make for desirable targets because “they love to talk about their business, and they love to talk about themselves,” Rinckey states. In these situations, he says, “you don't even really have to pry them that much.”.

#23902. The Smart Ring Goes to Church

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1362 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

The Smart Ring Goes to Church

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1362 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that stressed?
  • According to recent reports, the first generation of Christian smart rings is here, joining other religious wearables like iQibla’s dedicated Muslim smartwatches, rings, and Hajj bands alongside “kosher” smartwatch apps.
  • Everblessed’s $249 Elah Ring S1 went on sale in October and is shipping in the US.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that stressed? Heart rate elevated? If you’re wearing a smart ring from Oura, Ultrahuman, or Samsung, the spike could prompt app suggestions like breathing exercises, meditations, or a physical reset like a short walk. So far, so Silicon Valley. But now you can add reading the Bible to that list of self-soothing activities.

According to recent reports, the first generation of Christian smart rings is here, joining other religious wearables like iQibla’s dedicated Muslim smartwatches, rings, and Hajj bands alongside “kosher” smartwatch apps. Two latest devices in particular—Glorify’s Ring and Everblessed Technology’s Elah Ring—connect to hugely popular Christian prayer apps with tens of millions of users, and both claim to be the world’s first Christian smart ring.

Both are first, in their own ways. Everblessed’s $249 Elah Ring S1 went on sale in October and is shipping in the US. The $299 Glorify Ring launched in July, with reservations open and shipping set for January 2027, but 77,000 units of an earlier beta iteration, the Amen Ring made by faith tech firm ConfideIn (which merged with Glorify this May), were given away last Christmas. Everblessed manages the Blessed app, and Glorify has an eponymous app.

In a recent development, another major player in prayer apps is Hallow, aimed at Catholics, backed by Vice President JD Vance’s Narya venture capital firm and celebrity ambassadors, with 24 million installs to date. Hallow’s toe-dip into wearables was a 2024 smart rosary with NFC embedded in the crucifix, made with Italian brand Ghirelli; Everblessed tried an earbud, necklace, and bedside device before settling on the ring design.

Head-to-head on design, the Elah and Glorify rings are both made from titanium alloy, with a thorn-inspired twist for Glorify and a minimalist band featuring a cross for the Elah S1, which is also IP68 waterproof to 5 meters.

Industry observers note that for now, the Elah Ring is slightly techier: prayer reminders come via the cross, which glows via an LED, and “gentle” vibrations; these can pulse at certain times of day or be triggered by changes in heart rate and stress levels, picked up by a photoplethysmography (PPG) sensor. Glorify’s CEO Henry Costa tells WIRED these emotion-based reminders will land on the Glorify Ring in six months; for now, you can set the times of day you want prayer reminders, track heart rate, blood oxygen, stress, and sleep via the optical sensor.

Recent findings suggest that one addition to the Glorify Ring that Costa claims he personally uses “a lot” is recording prayers straight into the built-in mic. The ring has a light to signal when it's recording, and the app transcribes them. Everblessed CEO Ricky Xia says that, after consulting with pastors and users, the feeling was that voice notes on the ring were seen as “suspicious.” It’s available in-app, but most people don’t pray out loud, and too many features drain the battery life. (The Elah Ring runs for up to six days on one charge; Glorify for four to five days.).

Industry observers note that both companies see the smart ring nudges helping wearers prioritize meaningful quiet time, away from screens, while offering in-app Christian practices as an alternative to Eastern meditation. Glorify offers Bible study, courses, and meditations. Blessed has devotional “anchors,” Bible texts and audio, plus guided breathing. Xia claims he’s happy if the Elah vibrates and a user picks up a paper Bible rather than the Blessed app, while Costa says he’s “crying out to use my phone less.”.

Industry observers note that both Glorify (founded in 2020, now merged with ConfideIn and headquartered in the San Francisco Bay Area) and Blessed (founded in 2023 and based in San Jose) operate in more than 150 countries. Perhaps the biggest difference between the two rings is their relationship to AI.

In a recent development, xia is all-in, describing the S1 as an “AI-native” product, with a pastor-complementing, not-replacing FaithMate chatbot in the Blessed app, customized based on preferences, congregation, and depth of learning. ChatGPT is like a “good coworker,” he notes, while FaithMate is designed to be “your friend” and an agent that can also handle secular tasks.

“A lot of our owners not only ask questions about the Bible but also ask about themselves, their relationships with their wives, they’re being bullied at school," Xia says, stressing safeguards around data storage, encryption, and privacy. "Everyone is going to have some AI that they trust, and how they view that is built on their personal stuff, their private vulnerabilities.”.

Costa is more circumspect, treading carefully on the consumer-facing side and noting that the Pope has weighed in with a 6,000-word encyclical on AI. A launch interview with CBN News garnered negative comments: “AI is Antichrist Information,” for one.

Sources indicate that “The stance I’ve always taken is that our daily devotional is hand-authored by a team of theologians,” Costa says. “It’s prayed over, and that is a stamp of approval.” He criticizes AI slop prayer apps as inauthentic. Still, he says the Glorify team has already tested “many forms” of AI personalization: “Any time, if we do use AI, it must be very clear to the user.”.

Smart ring owners were finding ways to add faith features to mainstream accessories before these rings came to fruition. For 20 years, timer and reminder apps have helped with prayer schedules, but recent examples are more creative. Heidi Campbell, professor of communication in religious studies at Texas A&M, refers to these DIY upgrades to the Oura ring and devices like the Muse headband as “spiritual mind-body hacking.”.

Oura owners on #christiantiktok chat about how they already use the ring’s stress and HR alerts as a prompt to pause and reflect, as per Elah.

It has been revealed that smart ring consumers flag changes in resting heart rate and sleep quality with scripture following their daily practice. “It’s really helpful for, like, what was inhibiting me from getting to a meditative or contemplative prayer state?” Campbell states. “It takes some of the mystery out of prayer, I think, but that can also be positive. There is a way to do prayer well and not well.” Ring hackers can also dig into health stats during Lent, Ramadan, and Yom Kippur to analyze energy expenditure and how fasting periods affect their bodies.

According to recent reports, AI-powered voice recordings and emerging attempts at emotion tracking are part of a fresh phase for smart rings, says Ekta Mittal, a senior analyst of connected devices at CCS Insight. These new “purpose-driven” features extend wearable tech into “new parts of consumers’ daily routines,” Mittal says. She suggests that while Glorify and Everblessed will add value for some, the rings are “not directly competing” with established smart ring giants like Oura, Ultrahuman, and Samsung.

The pandemic sped up the digital transition of many places of worship when congregations could not meet up in person, encouraging experimentation with social media. So it’s early days for Silicon Valley’s impact on organized religion. Researchers at the University of Würzburg in Germany, led by Ilona Nord, are studying the theological implications of using tech, including smart rings, for spiritual practices, investigating which values are baked into secular devices and apps.

Recent findings suggest that campbell suggests many Christian groups haven’t stopped to consider the unintentional consequences of cultivating spirituality via personal tech. “All of these things are about individualizing the practice, which is good, but the challenges are for religions which are really focused on communal aspects,” she claims. Not everyone has the money or connectivity to access these gadgets, but also, more existentially, “it puts spiritual development over communal development.”.

Xia points to the Blessed app’s communities, including its Healing Room broadcast feature, which lets pastors go live with sermons. It's not in the Elah app yet, but it's on the roadmap. Costa states communal practice is a core pillar, highlighting the “social layer” of public notes made on Christian texts in-app and an upcoming Glorify Ring feature which will allow a user to pair their device with a family member’s ring: “When your loved one is feeling down, you’ll get a buzz to check in with them.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Building the âyoung personâs AGI labâ to unlock data efficient models, which we believe is the bottleneck to laddering up the next rung of AI intelligence.

Building the âyoung personâs AGI labâ to unlock data efficient models, which we believe is the bottleneck to laddering up the next rung of AI intelligence.

Sources indicate that sometimes you meet a founder who is so good that you want to back them no matter what they are working on. Just as rarely, you meet a organization whose vision is so singular, it feels both inevitable and differentiated at the same time. When I first sat down with Ben and Asher Spector to discuss Flapping Airplanes, I felt both of these to be true at once.

In a recent development, ben is a founder of Prod, which has quickly become one of the most powerful talent incubators in Silicon Valley. Asher, one year Benâs senior, is a former debate champion turned Stanford statistics Ph.D. The brothers have an eye for raw talent, and aged 25 and 26 respectively, they are building the âyoung personâs AGI lab.â Their co-founder Aidan Smith is a former founder and Thiel fellow who worked at Neuralink for three years while in college at Georgia Tech. Ben and Asher believe that raw talent â the type of people who would previously have gone on to do Ph.D.s or join quant firms â are the key to unlocking the next phase of AI development. This stands in sharp contrast to the approach of focusing on âbrand nameâ AI talent at any price, which seems so in vogue right now.

Industry observers note that there is something else that is countercultural about this lab too: they recognize that scale alone is not enough. Indeed, the lab is predicated on this notion. There is only one Internet, and weâve run out of it. Data is the bottleneck today to further AI scaling, not compute. Todayâs AI models are wildly inefficient, something that Dwarkesh Patel has recently hammered home in his interviews with Andrej Karpathy, Richard Sutton and others. Flapping Airplanes is dedicated to searching for a more data-efficient AI. The companyâs name is a nod to a more biological notion of machine intelligence.

It has been revealed that one of the fundamental debates right now in AI is around scaling vs. research. The scaling paradigm argues for dedicating a huge amount of societyâs resources, as much as the economy can muster, toward scaling up todayâs LLMs, in the hopes that this will lead to AGI. The research paradigm argues that we are 2-3 research breakthroughs away from an âAGIâ intelligence, and as a result, we should dedicate resources to long-running research, especially projects that may take 5-10 years to come to fruition.

Recent findings suggest that while the divide between these two schools of thought is far from absolute â research breakthroughs make compute investments more efficient, and GPUs are required for net new research â they each lead to different tradeoffs. A compute-first approach would prioritize cluster scale above all else, and would heavily favor short-term wins (on the order of 1-2 years) over long-term bets (on the order of 5-10 years). A research-first approach would spread bets temporally, and should be willing to make lots of bets that have a low absolute probability of working, but that collectively expand the search space for what is possible.

Industry observers note that one concern I have had is that by starving Ph.D. programs of talent, and by reallocating a lot of this talent to scale-oriented work (as opposed to fundamental research), we could actually push out the AGI timeline. As I noted in a previous blog post, âcorporate politics tends to favor in vogue, consensus ideas over more radical, unpopular ones â the very kinds of ideas that can take years to prove worthwhile, and which scientific breakthroughs often depend on.â Flapping Airplanes is explicitly intended to provide a Ph.D.-like experience â true research independence, long-time horizons â while bridging the pay gap between academia and Big Tech.

Recent findings suggest that one of the biggest learnings of the last decade in AI is the dramatic economic value of fundamental scientific progress. Since academia seems ill-suited to compete with Major Tech on this dimension right now, especially in AI, Flapping Airplanes is taking this into their own hands. And they are focused on precisely the problem that is likely to define the next wave of AI: building models inspired by the data efficiency of biology. With that as a north star, the firm will make bets in a variety of directions to get there.

Recent findings suggest that there are two coherent motives right now in AI. One is the profit motive, and this should inspire all application builders, given the tremendous opportunity ahead. As I have noted on many occasions, AI is so underpenetrated relative to the capability set available, it is likely to create a golden age for builders for many years to come. There is a large profit pool available, and we are in the very earliest stages of generating it.

Recent findings suggest that the second coherent motive in AI is AGI, predicated on the belief that now that weâve unlocked a machine intelligence, we should push toward upleveling that intelligence. Economically, progress in this direction is likely to be extremely valuable. The question is how to take on this objective in an efficient way, with a reasonable probability that resources invested will translate into long-term positive results. Flapping Airplanes is a pure play in that direction.

One of the most attractive aspects for me in partnering with Flapping Airplanes was the team. I have met nearly every candidate that has interviewed at Flapping Airplanes, and certainly every person the organization has hired. This is one of the best teams Iâve ever seen assembled at the beginning of such an ambitious journey.

There are two core beliefs that make Flapping Airplanes different for top talent:.

A belief that young people have always unlocked fundamental science in the past (Einstein was 26 during his âMiracle Yearâ).

A conviction that AI research is not a mystical domain for experts, but a domain learnable by anyone that is smart and ambitious.

Industry observers note that with just these two premises, Flapping Airplanes is at odds with a prestige-obsessed culture in the Valley right now. It is exactly this obsession with substance and with raw individual talent that made Ben so successful at Prod, and it is this âflame spottingâ ability that gives me confidence in the courageous effort that is now Flapping Airplanes.

If you are interested to join, please reach out to recruiting@flappingairplanes.com.

Latest Update: The 36 Best REI Holiday Sale Outdoor Deals (2026)

💡 Key Takeaways
  • REI's 2026 Holiday Sale kicked off November 13 and lasts until November 23.
  • Sources indicate that there are also sales at Backcountry.com and some of our favorite cottage industry brands like Six Moon Designs, Zenbivy, and more.
  • The 650 Down Jacket is one of the best budget three-season puffer jackets you can buy, more so at this price.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

REI's 2026 Holiday Sale kicked off November 13 and lasts until November 23. There are plenty of great deals to help you restock your backpacking, hiking, biking, camping, outdoor loving gear quiver. REI members can use the code HOLIDAY2026 to save an extra 20 percent off one full-price item and an extra 20 percent off one REI Outlet item. Below are the best deals on all our favorite tents, backpacks, sleeping bags, pads, cookware, outdoor apparel, and more.

Sources indicate that there are also sales at Backcountry.com and some of our favorite cottage industry brands like Six Moon Designs, Zenbivy, and more. Not sure what you need? Check out our many outdoor gear guides.

The 650 Down Jacket is one of the best budget three-season puffer jackets you can buy, more so at this price. At 10.9 ounces, it's reasonably lightweight and has large hand pockets and some very nice internal pockets for stashing a hat or gloves. The kids' version is also on sale in a nice yellow color that's handy for spotting your child in the snow.

The Ghost Whisperer Down Jacket is my top pick for a backpacking puffer jacket. It weighs just 6.7 ounces for a men's medium (7.3 ounces for the men's large I tested), packs down to a tiny little thing (stuffing into its own pocket), and the 1,000-fill-power goose down offers one of the best warmth-to-weight ratios on the market. The men's version is technically on sale right now, but the only size available is small and XXL.

Industry observers note that this is my favorite puffer jacket, especially in the shoulder seasons when temps dip a little lower. It features 4.5 ounces of 1,000-fill down (men’s medium), which is half the weight of the overall jacket. The internal TILT lining (short for Thermo Ionic Lining Technology) may or may not do anything; I haven't been able to devise an effective test, but even if it did nothing, the amount of 1,000-fill-power down combined with the scant weight makes this an appealing option for ultralighters. The 7D fabric (which is what keeps the weight low) does need babying, but I haven't had any concerns in over a year of use.

This is great deal on a very warm down parka. It's thigh-length, which helps keep drafts up your back to a minimum, and it fits pretty well, though it's definitely boxy (what do you want from a 650-down-fill parka that's designed primarily to keep you warm?). I did find that the main two-way zipper can be fiddly, and does sometimes snag, but it's hardly a deal-breaker, especially at this price.

This 850-fill down hoodie makes the honorable mentions section of our puffer jacket guide. The cut is roomy and its gusseted around the shoulders for climbing. Our main gripe is that it's pricey, but this deal takes some of sting out of the price. The women's version is unfortunately not on sale.

According to recent reports, the Rainier is our favorite budget rain jacket, especially when it's on sale. Unlike most rain jackets in this price range, the Rainier uses high-quality three-layer, seam-taped, laminate waterproofing that's non-fluorinated (meaning no PFAS). It has some other features rare in budget rain jackets, like pit zips or venting, a weatherproof center zip, and an adjustable, stowable hood.

It's a little weird to shop for sun hoodies with snow on the way, but if you're looking to avoid the sun next summer, REI's Sahara Shade hoodie is a great alternative to sunscreen. I don't often use a sun hoodie myself, but I have worn this one and it does do a good job of protecting you without feeling too stuffy on a hot day (it's definitely better for protecting against high altitude sun rather than humid, Florida sun).

When these were an REI Outlet deal earlier this year I got nervous that they might be discontinued, but apparently not because they are back. REI's 100 percent merino base layers are some of the best values around, even at full price. On sale, they're a true steal. I like this half-zip for the extra ventilation the zipper provides when I'm riding my bike, but if you prefer, the regular top is also on sale for $64, as is the base layer bottom.

Smartwool's 100 percent merino base layer is my top pick for cooler weather in our guide to the best base layers. It's a great all-around choice, and the loose fit makes it work as a long-sleeve T-shirt in the shoulder seasons. That extra bit of roominess makes it possible to use it as a second light layer over something thinner. The pants are also on sale for $94 ($31 off).

Recent findings suggest that keen's Targhee Apex has finally found a look that isn't bad by Targhee standards. Perhaps more than any other shoe we've tested, these look like the trail-running Gorpcore icons they are. At just 0.75 pounds each, they are light without being fragile, and the generous footbed lets your feet spread comfortably on long days.

According to recent reports, the La Sportiva Prodigio combines trail-running agility with boot-level protection, delivering surprising versatility on rugged terrain. They're one of our favorite light hiking boots. The fit is a little on the snug side—much like La Sportiva climbing shoes—but they should be fine even for wide feet thanks to the generous footbed width. At 1.65 pounds for the pair, these aren't terribly bulky, either.

It has been revealed that these are my favorite barefoot sandals. I always refer to these as the barefoot equivalent of Chaco sandals. They're not as robust—I'd still bring Chacos for white-water rafting—but for everything else, these are perfect. Z-Trails flex and bend as you walk, giving your feet the freedom of movement you'd expect from a barefoot shoe, though these do have 10 mm of cushioning, which makes them a good option if you're just starting out with barefoot shoes. The even more minimal Z-Trek sandals are also on sale for $45 ($15 off).

Industry observers note that these Fjällräven Vidda Pro trousers are my favorite hiking pants thanks the thigh zips that deliver excellent ventilation. The Vidda Pros uses Fjällräven's G-1000 fabric, a 65 percent recycled polyester and 35 percent cotton blend, with pockets everywhere, and nice reinforced knees (with openings for pads). There's even a hatchet loop on the leg.

Six Moon Design's Lunar Solo is one of the best single-wall ultralight solo tents you can buy. It's not without its quirks (read the pitching tips), but if you want something more than a tarp, that still weighs just 26 ounces (740 grams), this one is hard to beat. Use the Code YULEHIKE to get the 25 percent off.

Nemo's Hornet tents are some of the lightest freestanding tents around. The 1-person model is my go-to for situations where I might have to pitch on rock or concrete slabs (like staying in towns on a longer bike-packing trip). It's roomy enough for you and all your gear, light enough at 2.25 pounds (without stakes), and packs down remarkably small. It's also held up well in storms, though you will want some extra guy-outs if the wind is really howling (I like Zpacks 1.2-mm dyneema cord for lightweight guy lines).

This is the bike-packing version of Massive Agnes' popular Copper Spur tent, one of the best backpacking tents around. The only difference, aside from color, is that the pole segments on this model are shorter (to make it easier to store on a bike). The Copper Spur line is very nearly the lightest freestanding tent around (it's just slightly heavier than the Hornet above), and if you happen to use it with trekking poles, you get what I think is the best feature, the covered awning modification for the vestibule. While this is the best deal, the 2-person model is also on sale for 20 percent off.

This is one of my favorite ultralight sleeping bags. There are lighter quilts out there, but when you need the warmth of a mummy bag on those colder nights, this is what I use. It also has the smallest pack size of any bag I've tested in this temperature range. With the included compression sack, this thing is truly tiny. The down fill is PFC-free, 850+ hydrophobic down. The zippers are on the small side, but they slide well and rarely (if ever) snag on the bag. I've slept in this bag down to 20 degrees and never been the least bit cold.

Sources indicate that closed-cell foam pads like the Therm-a-Rest Z-Lite Sol are a must-have. They weigh next to nothing (10 ounces for the small), fold up small enough to lash to the outside of any pack, and double as a chair, extra padding on cold nights, table, you name it. I am too old and too soft to be the sort of ultra-minimalist who gets by with just a Z-Lite, but I still have one around on almost every trip I take.

Industry observers note that nemo's Tensor-insulated sleeping pads have the best R-value-to-weight ratio of anything I've tested. The Tensor All-Season featured here sports an R-value of 5.4 and weighs 18.2 ounces. That alone is impressive, but what I love about the Tensor is that it's thick, comfortable, and most importantly, nearly silent. The lighter Trail model is also on sale at REI. Its R-value is only 2.8, though.

In a recent development, I love my MegaMat, it is hands down the best sleeping experience I've had car camping (I have the auto version that fits in the back of your car). While it's not our absolute favorite mega sleeping pad (that's the slightly lighter, smaller MondoKing), I like the MegaMat better it has slightly better insulation. This deal is on the duo model, which is 72 inches long and 41 inches wide. The single wide MegaMat is also on sale for $195 ($75 off).

Recent findings suggest that I don't usually bring a chair backpacking—I just sit on the ground. But for some reason, I do love a chair when I'm bike packing, which is where I've used this Nemo the most. It's quite pricey, but it's very light and packs down to a tiny package. The genius part of this chair is that the cover is also a mat that keeps it from sinking into soft ground.

According to recent reports, the thing to keep in mind when you shop REI-brand gear is the manufacturer's basic proposition: You get 90 percent of the designer item for 70 percent of the price. It's a strategy that works quite well and has generated some really great, affordable gear. This chair is a good example of that. It's not as nice as the Nemo above—it does wobble a bit, side to side, when you move—but it's still comfortable and half the price.

Sources indicate that this camp chair is the coziest way to hang out around the fire. It is a bit significant, heavy, and awkward to fold up and carry, but so long as you have room for it in your vehicle, there's no better way to relax under the stars with your loved ones.

Recent findings suggest that I sincerely hope you never have any need for one of these Sea to Summit bug head nets, but if you do, boy do you. I once did not have one and tried to go backpacking in Michigan’s UP in early May. I lasted about two hours. When I got home, I bought one of these and … still haven't ventured back to that marshy bog of a hike. But I could, and possibly even retain some of my sanity thanks to this thing.

Industry observers note that what I noted about the chair above goes for this day pack as well; it's an excellent value, especially on sale. I was surprised by how comfortable this thing is, especially because, to look at it, the straps are very lightweight and there's almost no padding. It still managed to carry loads up to 10 pounds without straining my shoulders, and the side stash pockets are fabulously large—big enough for a Nalgene bottle or rain jacket. The Flash 22 is made of 70-denier recycled ripstop nylon, which is on the lighter side, but mine has held up well, even coming through some rough canyon hikes in Utah without any more than mud stains.

These two pots are my go-to cooking vessels for larger group meals. I find they're just about perfect for boiling up enough water to rehydrate four servings. I don't take the bowls and silverware into the backcountry, but they're handy for camping.

According to recent reports, sure, phones have some of the features you'll get with a satellite messenger, but we still think you're better off with a dedicated device. Garmin's upcoming inReach Mini 3 Plus now offers some of those phone features—like voice messaging—along with the emergency features and excellent service worldwide. It's also still tiny, well-built, and it has great battery life. A non-Plus model, which doesn't have a speaker and mic, is also on sale.

The Stash is our favorite all-in-one backcountry cook system. The heat diffuser design is what speeds up boil times (Jetboil claims 2.5 minutes, which I was only able to match indoors in still air), but the real appeal here to me is the way this kit all packs down into itself. For weekend trips, this is the simplest system I've tested when it comes to cooking for two.

It has been revealed that jetboil's larger all-in-one cooking system, the Flash, offers a larger-capacity 1-liter pot that combines an integrated pot and burner into an easy-to-use system. I prefer the more compact Stash above, but if you're cooking for two and are all-in on dehydrated meals, this stove is popular for good reason.

In a recent development, these dry bags from Sea to Summit have double-stitched, tape-sealed seams that have held up well over the years. I also really like the external lash loops that make it easy to strap to anything with a tie-down anchor.

I like these dry bags for organizing things in my pack. They're not dry bags in the sense that you can submerge them and your gear will be fine, but the 30D silnylon with PCF-free DWR easily sheds a little rain. And they make finding your stuff easy. I put all my cooking gear in a red bag (red for fire), all my water-filtering stuff in a blue bag for, wait for it, water—and so on. I find the 3- and 5-liter bags the most useful, but you can get all the way up to 35L.

According to recent reports, I've noticed that, when trying to lighten their load with a smaller, lighter-weight backpack, people then struggle to fit all their gear. The answer for sleeping bags and clothing is this compression stuff sack, which takes my favorite sleeping bag (the Sea to Summit Spark above) and smashes it down to about half the size of the included stuff sack. You can do the same thing to clothing, especially puffer jackets, but also fleece and merino to some extent, to free up more room in your pack.

REI’s Major Haul duffel is a durable, water-resistant, gear-swallowing bag for carrying, well, just about everything. It's one of our favorite ways to schlep your gear when flying. It hits the right balance of robust build materials and pockets without being too heavy to lug around all day. The strap system is cleverly customizable, and you can convert it to a backpack.

Industry observers note that once upon a time, in a galaxy far, far away, I traveled around Southeast Asia with an early version of this Osprey pack, living out of it for almost a year. It stood up well to the abuse of overland travel—more than once, I watched a bus driver tie it to the roof of a bus by cinching it down with a rope, pulling with all his weight right down the middle of my pack, like a cheese cutter. The Farpoint survived, and my gear inside did as well, thanks in part to the thickly padded sides, which provide considerable extra cushioning.

1,190,000. Thatâs the number of road traffic deaths in a year. They are a leading cause of death for children and young adults worldwide.
